TI Comprehensive Evaluation of Large Language Models on Four Core Medical
   School Courses: A Cross-Sectional Comparative Study
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE large language models; medical education; artificial intelligence;
   medical school examinations; assessment integrity
AB Purpose: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical education, yet their performance on discipline-specific medical school course examinations remains incompletely characterized. This study evaluated six contemporary LLMs on final examinations for four core medical school courses: Surgery, Musculoskeletal System Diseases, Digestive System Diseases, and Respiratory System Diseases. Methods: A total of 400 multiple-choice questions (100 per course) were administered to each model. Responses were scored against official answer keys and compared to the performance of 312 medical students. Each question was tested three times per model to assess response consistency and reproducibility. Results: All six LLMs achieved mean scores exceeding 93% across all four courses, substantially outperforming the student cohort mean of 71.8%, with all models scoring above the 99.5(th )percentile of the student score distribution. ChatGPT 5.5 achieved the highest overall accuracy (97.0%), followed by Claude Opus 4.7 (96.3%) and DeepSeek V4 (95.8%). Qwen 3.7 (95.3%) and GLM 5.2 (94.3%) demonstrated comparable performance, while Doubao 2.1 (93.8%) showed the lowest but still exceptional accuracy. A sensitivity analysis revealed that accuracy on the 12 visual-containing questions was substantially lower (50.0%) than on text-only questions (96.8%). All models demonstrated high response consistency (kappa = 0.82-0.95) and reproducibility (>95%). Conclusions: Contemporary LLMs can achieve near-perfect performance on medical school course examinations, substantially exceeding average student performance. While this capability suggests significant potential for LLMs as supplementary educational tools, it also raises important concerns regarding assessment integrity and the appropriate role of AI in medical training.

TI A Bibliometric Sketch of Research Paradigm Shifts and Divides: The Case
   of Race and Education Scholarship
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Race; Artificial Intelligence; Critical Theory; Philosophy; Research
   Methodology; Descriptive Analysis; Axiology; Research Paradigm;
   Ontology; Epistemology; Quantitative Criticism; Large Language Models;
   GenAI
ID MIXED METHODS; SOCIOLOGY; PREVALENCE; PRAGMATISM; QUESTION
AB Grounded in ontology and axiology, this research develops a taxonomy to analyze research paradigms. The taxonomy is then applied to the field of race and K-12 education in the United States. Using a large language model (Gemini 2.0) for automated classification, 15,585 research abstracts published between 1970 and 2024 are classified to trace paradigm shifts across the past five decades according to their ontological and axiological stances. The findings reveal a marked transition from the dominance of non-value-committed realist paradigms to the growing prevalence of value-committed constructivist approaches in this field. Complementing this analysis, citation and co-citation network mapping shows that paradigm divides strongly correspond to researchers' ontological and axiological orientations, which often underlie the differences in research methods. The article concludes by underscoring the importance of epistemological pluralism and epistemic reflexivity as strategies to bridge paradigm divides and foster more inclusive knowledge production.

TI Writing Beyond the Gaze: Writer Identity Construction in Black Women's
   Personal Statements to Doctoral Programs
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Black women; doctoral admissions; personal statements; graduate
   education; storytelling
ID GENRE STRUCTURE; ADMISSIONS; DISCOURSE; STUDENTS; PURPOSE; WRITTEN
AB Recognizing the increasingly significant role of personal statements in graduate admissions, this qualitative study explores how Black women applicants engaged in writer identity construction in their statements to PhD programs across STEM, social science, and humanities disciplines. By examining the scripts and schemas that underpin this mundane activity, we highlight how Black women's rhetorical and language choices offer insight into the racialized and gendered performance of merit in graduate admissions. Our analysis of 19 semistructured interviews and 56 personal statements revealed three themes detailing how Black women applicants to PhD programs shaped their writer identity construction while navigating the white gaze: a) writing in response to racialized institutional identity; b) resisting damage-centered narratives; and c) positioning Black womanhood as separate from scholarly identities. Overall, the study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complexities of storytelling faced by Black women applicants in graduate education and underscores the need for equitable admissions practices that acknowledge and mitigate these challenges.

TI Tolerance of Teachers in Ukraine's Educational Landscape Amidst War
SO REVISTA BRASILEIRA DE EDUCACAO DO CAMPO-BRAZILIAN JOURNAL OF RURAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE tolerance; education; teacher; educational institution
AB The military aggression by the Russian Federation against Ukraine has resulted in civilian casualties, the destruction of infrastructure, and large-scale internal migration, significantly impacting the education system. In this context, the issue of tolerance has become increasingly relevant. This study aimed to assess the level and types of tolerance among Ukrainian educators during wartime. A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted with 150 educators from July to October 2024 using a structured self-reported questionnaire. The research tools included the "Tolerance Index" express questionnaire and the "Types and Components of Tolerance-Intolerance" scale. Statistical analysis revealed that most educators equate tolerance with indulgence, while over a third understand it as an active, respectful stance toward self and others. High levels of development were observed in interpersonal, managerial, intercultural, interfaith, intergenerational, gender, professional, and interethnic tolerance. In contrast, socio-economic and political tolerance showed average development. The overall tolerance index among education professionals was found to be at an average level, with the highest indicators noted in interpersonal, managerial, and intergenerational domains. The findings highlight the complex nature of tolerance in crisis conditions and underscore the need for targeted support and training in educational settings.

TI Factors Associated with Dropout Intentions in Vocational Education and
   Training
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Vocational training; school dropouts; school integration; motivation;

ID STUDENTS; CAREER
AB The study focuses on exploring the transition processes of students enrolled in Vocational Education and Training (CINE-3) and deepening the analysis of the interaction of factors among those who show clear intentions to drop out of their VET programs. A multiple case study was conducted involving nine VET centers across different autonomous communities. A closed-ended questionnaire was administered to a total of 2,161 intermediate and advanced VET students, with a sampling error of 1.2%. The findings highlight the importance of guidance services at this educational stage, as they may prevent the crystallization of dropout intentions into actual withdrawal.

TI Equity and training of mathematics teachers: a study using TIMSS 2019
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE primary school teachers; primary teacher education; teaching practice;
   mathematics; assessment; educational needs; social justice; Primary
   education
ID EDUCATION
AB Teacher training constitutes a key element in addressing educational inequalities, as it allows teachers to update their knowledge and employ pedagogical approaches that respond effectively to the diversity of students in their classrooms. Drawing on the results obtained from TIMSS 2019 in Spain, two indicators-an outcome inequity indicator and an opportunity inequity indicator-were obtained to select the least and most inequitable schools from the sample. Based on this selection, teaching variables regarding the need for future development activities in mathematics were analyzed, obtaining evidence on the existence or not of differences between schools depending on their level of inequity. The results indicate that primary education mathematics teachers in Spain, regardless of the school's equity level, generally present high training needs regarding pedagogy, ICT integration, the improvement of students' critical thinking or problem-solving skills, assessment, and addressing individual needs; conversely, there is a lower perceived need in terms of curriculum and content in the subject area. Despite the existence of significant differences between the two types of schools-less and more inequitable-in some variables, the effect sizes are generally very low. Nevertheless, the need for teacher professional development is evidenced as a fundamental key to the teaching profession in primary education.

TI Generative AI in Online Higher Education: Usage Profiles, Perceptions,
   and Relationship with Learning
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; distance education; higher education; digital
   divide; learning; student attitudes; educational technology; digital
   literacy
AB Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is transforming online higher education, though its adoption varies significantly among students. This study analyzes the profiles of online university students based on their use, perception, and adaptation to GAI, assessing the perceived relationship between these variables and their learning processes. The research employs a quantitative approach with a descriptive-correlational design and cluster analysis, applying an ad hoc questionnaire to a non-probabilistic, convenience sample of 69 students that measures frequency of use, perceived impact, technological confidence, and adaptive readiness. The results reveal two differentiated profiles of an exploratory nature, where age emerges as the primary differentiating factor. One profile, consisting of older students, shows selective use and lower adaptive readiness, while the second, significantly younger profile is characterized by early adoption and more frequent and flexible use in their academic practice. No significant differences are observed in overall perception or confidence towards GAI, suggesting a gap between positive theoretical valuation and practical implementation. It is concluded that the effective integration of GAI requires targeted interventions, such as digital literacy programs for older students and the redesign of assessment systems that foster critical thinking and ethical collaboration with technology among younger students.

TI Photointervention and children's agency in rural schools in territories
   affected by socio-environmental crisis
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE childhood; student participation; rural education; environment;
   ecological crisis; photographs; intervention; Chile
AB The article presents a study on children's agency in school and rural contexts affected by socio-environmental crisis from a sociomaterial perspective and within the framework of the Social Studies of Childhood. The aim of the article is to examine how girls and boys attending rural schools articulate affects, materialities, and territories in their narratives about the socio-environmental crisis. A participatory methodological design was employed through the technique of photointervention with a total of 24 students aged 9 to 13 from three rural schools located in different territories affected by water crises, extractivism, and ecological degradation in Chile. The methodology included analogue photographic production, collective narratives, and spaces for reflection oriented toward action. The findings portray verbal and visual narratives that articulate affects, materialities, and territories, revealing an agency distributed among children, images, objects, nature, and landscape. The socio-environmental crisis is understood through everyday experiences and translated into proposals for care, denunciation, and collective transformation. The discussion addresses the place of children's agency in their learning processes within schools, as well as the need for pedagogical and multimodal dispositifs capable of producing emergent forms of agency from childhood perspectives and from a sociomaterial understanding.

TI Design and validation of an instrument to assess co-teaching
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA English
DT Article
DE Team teaching; Teacher collaboration; Teaching methods; Educational
   assessment; Questionnaires
ID MODEL; SUPPORT
AB This study aims to design and validate a questionnaire that enables the measurement of co-teaching development among Spanish non-university teachers, considering both its phases-planning, instruction (based on co-teaching structures), assessment, and reflection-and its interpersonal dimensions: parity, interaction, and communication. For the initial design, an exhaustive review of the literature and an analysis of conceptual frameworks on co-teaching were first conducted. Subsequently, the questionnaire underwent qualitative content validation through the judgment of national and international experts, using an ad hoc 10-item Likert-scale instrument. Agreement among experts was analyzed using Fleiss' Kappa and the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient across four scenarios, showing moderate agreement and good reliability. These phases determined that DOCEN-CO consisted of 34 items distributed across six dimensions with asymmetric Likert scales, both in the number of items and the number of response levels, to adequately adapt to the particularities of each dimension. DOCEN-CO was quantitatively validated in its final form using a representative sample of 1,521 participants via a Robust Slightly Restricted Confirmatory Factor Analysis (RMR-CFA) to avoid the inherent bias of simple classical factor analysis. The results demonstrate excellent overall psychometric properties (CFI = 0.999; TLI = 0.999; RMSEA = 0.012), indicating that DOCEN-CO is a robust and reliable instrument for assessing co-teaching among teachers from diverse professional backgrounds.

TI Reading the World from Epistemic Justice: Transliterary Conversation and
   the Picturebook
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Epistemic justice; transliterary conversation; multimodal literacy;
   picturebook; reader training; educational inclusion; primary education;
   Zones with Needs for Social Transformation (ZTS)
ID LITERACY; BOOK
AB This article defines, justifies and analyses the impact of mediated "transliterary conversation" on picturebooks for the development of epistemic justice and the right to reading in vulnerable school contexts. The research was conducted in a 4th-grade primary classroom in a Zone with Needs for Social Transformation (ZTS) in Seville. The methodological design was structured into eleven sessions divided into two thematic blocks: Death and War & migration. The study concludes that transliterary conversation constitutes a key tool for educational inclusion and the exercise of citizenship from childhood, transforming the classroom into a space for symbolic participation and equity.

TI Sociodemographic, digital and academic factors associated with
   nomophobia among university students
SO REVISTA FUENTES
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE higher education; university student; internet; mobile phone; ict;
   academic performance; social problem; media education
AB The intensive use of smartphones has fostered the emergence of phenomena such as nomophobia, understood as the discomfort or anxiety associated with being unable to access or use this device. In the university context, this issue has become highly relevant due to its potential implications for students' digital well-being and academic experience. The present study analysed the prevalence of nomophobia among higher education students, as well as differences across its four dimensions (not being able to access information, giving up convenience, not being able to communicate, and loss of connection) according to gender, age, daily frequency of Internet use, and academic performance. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and ex post facto design based on the survey method was employed, with a sample of 1,922 students from a public university in Spain. The results placed nomophobia at a moderate overall level, although 21.3% of participants were concentrated in the risk and problematic levels. The highest-scoring dimension was not being able to communicate. Significant differences were also identified according to gender, age, and daily Internet use, with the latter emerging as the strongest predictor in the regression models (R-2 = .048-.095). It is concluded that nomophobia warrants attention from a psychoeducational and preventive perspective in higher education.

TI Semantic Network Analysis of Web Based Learning in Digital Health and
   Medical Education: A Scientometric Study with Mixed Methods and
   Systematic Mapping
SO SPANISH JOURNAL OF MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Web based learning; E learning; Digital health; Medical education;
   Learning analytics; Semantic network analysis; Scientometrics
AB Objectives: To examine the semantic and structural organization of web based learning at the intersection of digital health and medical education and to identify core, thematic, and bridging concepts within the knowledge network. Methods: A scientometric mixed methods design was applied to 1,123 peer reviewed articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 2016 to 2025. Bibliographic records were normalized and analyzed using co occurrence and thematic network analysis in VOSviewer and centrality analysis in UCINET and NetDraw. Temporal mapping and systematic semantic interpretation were used to examine convergence, thematic organization, and strategic conceptual positions. Results: The knowledge structure showed a strong educational backbone centered on e learning, education, and medical education, with learning analytics, digital literacy, artificial intelligence, machine learning, telemedicine, and digital health increasingly connected within the same conceptual environment. Thematic analysis indicated three interconnected domains comprising educational and pedagogical, technological and informatics, and clinical and digital health concepts. Closeness and betweenness centrality further distinguished structurally accessible core concepts from potential interdisciplinary bridging concepts. Conclusion: Web based learning has developed from a primarily instructional mechanism into an interconnected digital learning ecosystem linking medical education, intelligent technologies, informatics, and healthcare applications. The findings highlight the importance of understanding both conceptual prominence and structural position when examining the evolution of digital health education.

DE clinical reasoning; curriculum development; technology-enhanced

AB Purpose: To describe self-reported artificial intelligence (AI) use and perceptions of benefits, risks, and curricular integration among medical students with previous AI contact at a Brazilian public university. Methods: This descriptive cross-sectional survey included a convenience sample of 189 students aged 18 years or older in Years 1-4 of medical school who reported previous contact with AI tools applied to medical education. Data were collected from March to July 2026 using a researcher-developed electronic questionnaire without formal validation and summarized descriptively using available responses. Results: Daily or weekly academic AI use was reported by 76.2% (144/189). Exposure to AI as a learning resource in a course was reported by 38.3% (72/188). Perceived improvement in differential diagnosis was reported by 57.8% (108/187), whereas 60.3% (114/ 189) perceived a risk of harmful dependence affecting human clinical judgment. Optional and controlled curricular integration was preferred by 72.0% (136/189). Conclusion: Among respondents with previous AI contact, frequent use coexisted with perceived benefits and concerns about dependence. These findings can support local discussion and further educational evaluation but do not establish objective learning effects or determine appropriate curricular approaches.

TI Video-Assisted Simulation with Audience Response (VASAR): An
   Educationally Efficient and Scalable Model for Medical Education
   Simulation
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE simulation learning; high-fidelity simulation; medical education; video;
   audience response system
ID OTOLARYNGOLOGY-HEAD; NECK-SURGERY; CURRICULUM; SYSTEM; SKILLS
AB Purpose: High-fidelity simulation offers invaluable educational benefits in medical education. It provides the opportunity to develop critical communication and crisis resource management skills, but depends upon a high level of resources including technical equipment, a simulated environment, and instructors with expertise in simulation. This study aimed to develop an educational model that provided some of the benefits of simulation but with increased educational efficiency. Methods: The intervention was implemented at a specialty continuing medical education conference. This study combined video scenarios, role-playing, team-based learning strategies, and audience response systems to create Video-Assisted Simulation with Audience Response (VASAR). Post-session questionnaire data was compared between traditional high-fidelity simulation and VASAR. Data was also compared to questionnaire responses from separate experiences with high-fidelity simulation. Results: The study included 70 participants. The data suggest that participants found VASAR to be useful (96%) and realistic (92%). Both video and audience response systems were felt to be valuable (96% and 92%). Participants indicated the workshop would help them practice more safely (80%). In comparison of VASAR with traditional high-fidelity simulation, there were no statistical differences for usefulness of the course (p=0.53), feedback from debriefers (p=0.14), or recommending the course to colleagues (p=0.48). Conclusion: This study suggests that Video-Assisted Simulation with Audience Response can provide an interactive simulated clinical experience which participants find useful to clinical practice, and that VASAR can provide a tool for future strategies in medical education. Plain Language Summary: Traditional high-fidelity simulation provides many educational benefits but requires heavy resources and instructor expertise. Video-Assisted Simulation with Audience Response (VASAR) utilizes videos, role-playing, team-based learning strategies, and audience response systems to provide some of the benefits of simulation, but with increased educational efficiency. Participants found VASAR to be interactive, to simulate real-life settings, and to provide useful feedback through debriefing. There were no statistically significant differences noted between VASAR and traditional simulation in this study. VASAR can provide a useful model for remote and distributed medical education with a scalable audience that can be used for the medical education of the future.

TI The Estimated Effects of Waiving English Learner Services on
   Course-Taking and Graduation
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Bilingual/Bicultural; Educational Policy; High Schools;
   Quasi-Experimental Analysis
ID SOCIAL CAPITAL FRAMEWORK; STUDENTS; OPPORTUNITY; TRACKING; ACCESS
AB A nascent body of research has begun to explore the characteristics of students whose families waive English learner (EL) services and the relationship between waiving EL services and student outcomes. Drawing on longitudinal student-level data from Oregon, we used coarsened exact matching to provide the first estimated effects of waiving EL services on course-taking and graduation. We found that waiving resulted in students taking fewer English Language Development credits, fewer credits overall, and, in most models, more elective credits. For students who waived EL services specifically in 12th grade, we found large, statistically significant increases in the odds of graduating and receiving a regular diploma, as well as a meaningful reduction in the odds of pushout. However, looking across all high school years, waiving EL services at any point in high school had no significant effect on most graduation and pushout outcomes. We discuss implications for policy and practice.

TI Pharmacy Students' Perceptions of the Objective Structured Clinical
   Examination in Jordan: A Cross-Sectional Study at Two Universities
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE objective structured clinical examination; OSCE; pharmacy education;
   student perception; clinical assessment
ID EXAMINATION OSCE; COMPETENCE; EXAMINERS; DOCTOR
AB Background: The Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) is a widely used assessment tool in pharmacy education because of its structured and standardized approach. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate pharmacy students' perceptions of the OSCE experience in Jordan, and to assess the difference in perceptions based on GPA category. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among Bachelor of Pharmacy and Doctor of Pharmacy students at the University of Jordan and Jordan University of Science and Technology. A total of 236 students who had previously completed at least one OSCE were recruited using convenient sampling between March and May 2025. Data were collected using a validated questionnaire that assessed four domains: OSCE attributes, performance and implementation, scoring, objectivity and feedback, and educational outcomes. Responses were measured using a five-point Likert scale, and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods. Results: Students reported generally neutral to slightly positive perceptions of the OSCE. More than half of the respondents (51.3%) perceived the examination as stressful, while perceptions regarding scoring objectivity and feedback quality varied. Approximately one-quarter of participants (28.3%) reported that the allocated time per station was inadequate. Most participants recognized the educational value of the OSCE in increasing awareness of potential dispensing and counseling errors. Bivariate analyses showed that students with higher GPAs reported significantly more positive perceptions regarding pre-examination preparation and station timing than those with lower GPAs (p-value < 0.05). Conclusion: Students reported generally neutral to slightly positive perceptions of the OSCE. Most participants acknowledged the role of OSCE in increasing awareness of potential dispensing and counselling errors. However, concerns remained regarding examination-related stress and scoring objectivity. These findings highlight areas for future prospective, longitudinal, and multistakeholder research aimed at further evaluating and refining the OSCE process.

TI Perceived Barriers and Misconceptions Regarding Internal Medicine
   Residency Selection: A Pre-Post Survey Evaluation of a "Path to
   Specialization" Speed Dating Event
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE medicine; specialization; transparency; barriers; residency
ID EDUCATION
AB Introduction: To explore transparency and address misconceptions regarding the selection of medical residents, the Internal Medicine Department of the Erasmus Medical Center, Rotterdam, The Netherlands, organized a "path to specialization" event. This event targeted medical bachelor's and master's students, PhD candidates, and junior doctors who consider a residency training in internal medicine. The event featured a plenary opening, followed by structured speed-dating sessions with internal medicine physicians and residents, fostering open discussions in an interactive question-and-answer format. In the current study, we evaluated the effects of this event on (mis)conceptions about selection procedures and explored whether it could help reduce perceived barriers. Methods: Participants completed a full questionnaire before the event and a shortened post-event questionnaire repeating the three belief statements and two open-ended questions. The questionnaires were anonymous and therefore the statistical analyses were unpaired as the responses could not be linked. Results: A total of 60 participants were included in the current study, of whom 38 (63%) reported obstacles in choosing internal medicine as their specialty of choice. Following the speed-dating sessions, participants reported greater perceived transparency and fewer misconceptions regarding residency selection compared with before the event. The median self-estimated likelihood of being accepted into an internal medicine residency increased from 6 (IQR 5-7) before the event to 7 (IQR 6-8) after the event (p<0.001). Agreement with the statement that "a PhD is required to enter internal medicine residency" decreased from 6 (IQR 5-7) to 4 (IQR 3-6) (p<0.01). Similarly, agreement with the statement that "outside the conurbation it is easier to enter internal medicine residency training" decreased from 6 (IQR 4-8) to 3 (IQR 2-4) (p< 0.0001). Additionally, participants identified key areas for improvement that could enhance the attractiveness of internal medicine as a specialty, including the need for a mentor or role model, with 38/60 attendees reporting this need (62%). Discussion: Speed date sessions may represent a feasible approach to improving transparency, addressing misconceptions, and supporting prospective applicants in residency selection. Such interventions might be particularly valuable in systems with open, competitive selection such as the Netherlands, and may also help address application inflation in matching-based systems, such as in the United States, by aligning applicant expectations with selection processes. Longitudinal prospective studies are warranted to further evaluate the potential effects of this approach.

TI Social Networks From the Margins: Race, Social Capital, and Educational
   Access Among Youth Experiencing Homelessness
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE At-risk students; families; poverty; networking; social class; urban
   education; in-depth interviewing; qualitative research; case studies;
   student homelessness; social capital; Black homelessness
ID STUDENTS
AB More than 1.5 million U.S. students are identified as experiencing homelessness each year, yet many remain disconnected from school-based protections. This study offers a race-conscious analysis of how Black and Latine youth experiencing homelessness access institutional and alternative forms of capital across fragmented systems of support. Drawing on interviews with 23 youth in Los Angeles County, the study uses Lin's social capital theory and Stanton-Salazar's concept of empowerment agents. Findings show that housing and antipoverty systems were often disconnected from McKinney-Vento protections. Institutional mistrust and concerns about racialized surveillance discouraged some youth from disclosing housing instability. Familial and community-based networks provided material assistance, emotional support, and day-to-day stability through relational logics of care, but did not consistently connect youth to formal educational protections. Findings demonstrate that support and access are complementary, not synonymous.

AB Creative giftedness gained a foothold in American K-12 schools with the inception of the Marland report. TI A cluster concept for giftedness, creativity, and situated cognition
SO GIFTED EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Gifted education; identification; creativity; 4E cognition; cluster
   concept; situated cognition; practically able
ID ABILITY; ACCELERATION; IMPACT
AB Many definitions exist to define giftedness. A common denominator in these definitions is that they are 'classical theories of concepts' based on a set of necessary and sufficient conditions. As a result, a clear borderline is drawn between those belonging to the category and those outside, supposedly making identification of gifted students easy. In this article, a new way of defining giftedness is suggested by a cluster concept. In addition, the article argues that giftedness is situated - a property of the individual in the environment. These two factors are judged to have significance for understanding giftedness in relation to students who are at risk of being left without provision, such as creative students who perform well in a practical setting. Above all, the paper challenges the idea of provision being based on identification which is based on definition. Instead, it is argued that identification should take place within provision.

AB The recognised educational opportunities to stimulate children's creative potential make the early identification of creativity an important research challenge. The aim of the present study was to investigate the creative potential of school-aged children in France and Slovenia. The Evaluation of Potential Creativity (EPoC) battery was used to measure creative potential through eight divergent-exploratory and convergent-integrative creative thinking tasks in the graphic and verbal domains. The results show that creative giftedness is rather rare according to the type of thinking process (divergent vs. integrative), and it is best characterised by a domain-specific approach to creativity (verbal vs. graphic) compared to four EPoC thinking process-domain specific indices, regardless of the educational context. Finally, tailored educational interventions are proposed to promote children's creativity

TI The Impact of Emotional Intelligence on Gifted and Talented Students'
   Creative Problem-Solving Performance
SO GIFTED EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE creative giftedness; creative problem-solving; emotional intelligence;
   gifted and talented students
ID MODEL; THINKING; ABILITY
AB Creativity, a core 21st-century competency, is widely recognized as essential in gifted education but is often overshadowed in practice by a focus on academic and intellectual metrics, limiting the identification and nurturing of creative potential. This study examines the influence of emotional intelligence (EQ), defined by the Bar-On model, on creative problem-solving (CPS) performance in gifted and talented students. Seven creatively gifted students from a Science and Art Center in T & uuml;rkiye-identified for exceptional potential in biology-participated. EQ was assessed using the Bar-On EQ-i:YV, covering Intrapersonal, Interpersonal, Adaptability, and Stress Management dimensions. CPS performance was evaluated across Problem Formulation, Solution Formulation, and Solution Implementation phases over five sessions, yielding a Composite Creativity score for fluency and flexibility. Non-parametric analyses (Spearman's rho, Theil-Sen regression) revealed significant positive correlations between Total EQ and CQ scores across all CPS phases. Furthermore, EQ strongly predicted CPS performance, accounting for a moderate portion of the variance in Problem Formulation, a larger portion in Solution Formulation, and a particularly significant portion in Solution Implementation. Specific EQ dimensions like Adaptability demonstrated consistent influence, while Interpersonal and Stress Management skills were particularly critical in the Solution Implementation phase. Despite the small sample, the results underscore the value of integrating EQ and social-emotional learning into gifted education to support the holistic development of creatively gifted students. Future research should examine larger samples and individual EQ dimensions to deepen understanding of this relationship.

TI Brazilian Creatively Gifted Adults: Are There Gender Differences?
SO GIFTED EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE giftedness; talent; creativity; gender; bias
ID TESTS; THINKING
AB Gender differences in highly creative individuals need to be investigated. In two samples of Brazilian people with high levels of creativity, gender differences were investigated. First, 335 adults responded to a set of figural and verbal tests. A total of 64 individuals were identified using +1SD above the mean (30 women, 34 men) and 19 using +2SD (9 women, 10 men). A second sample of 711 adults was tested for their figural creativity. 96 participants had +1 SD above the mean (69 women, 27 men) and 24 had +2 SD above the mean (17 women, 7 men). There were no significant gender differences in total creativity scores between the groups in both samples for the two-creativity level based on the Mann-Whitney test. According to these findings, educators must encourage women to express their creativity to achieve in all careers to combat gender bias.

TI Creative Climate and Motivation for Learning in the 1st Cycle of
   Elementary Education: A Comparative Study Between Gifted and Typically
   Developing Students
SO GIFTED EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; motivation; gifted; primary education; inclusive education
ID EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE
AB This study analyses the differences between gifted students and students with typical development with regard to the creative climate in the classroom and motivation for learning in the first Cycle of Elementary Education in Portugal. The sample included 74 students (40 typical development and 34 gifted), aged between 7 and 10 years. Two instruments validated in the Portuguese context were used: the "Climate for Creativity in the Classroom Scale" (Dias, 2014) and the "Motivation to Learn Assessment Scale" (EMA) (Neves & Boruchovitch, 2007), which enabled a detailed analysis of students' perceptions of creativity in teaching practices and the underlying motivational factors. The study sought to understand how the educational environment influenced various dimensions of motivation-intrinsic and extrinsic-in the two groups of students. It also aimed to identify differentiating elements that can guide teaching practices that are better suited to the needs of gifted students. The results showed that gifted students had a higher perception of their creativity and autonomy, while typical students showed higher levels of intrinsic motivation. No significant differences were found in interest in learning and support for the expression of ideas. Positive correlations were identified between creative climate factors and motivation, especially in gifted students, where extrinsic motivation was related to support for the expression of ideas and interest in learning. This suggests that a creative environment can foster both motivation and the development of cognitive and socio-emotional skills, encouraging meaningful learning that is appropriate to the specificities of each profile.

TI Development of Self-Observation Assessment Rubrics to Improve Teacher
   Competency in Creative Gifted Education
SO GIFTED EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE self-observation; assessment rubrics; teacher competency; gifted
   education; reflective practice; creativity
AB The purpose of this study was to develop self-observation assessment metrics and rubrics for teachers in gifted education, with a particular emphasis on nurturing creativity. The objective of the developed metrics and rubrics is to facilitate systematic self-evaluation, promote reflective practice, and support continuous instructional improvement. TI Assessing Socio-Motor Creativity in Team Sports: An Ecological Framework
   for Identifying Creative Potential
SO GIFTED EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE socio-motor creativity; team sports; ecological assessment; praxical
   communication; motor decision making; creative potential; observational
   protocol
ID VALIDITY; CONSTRAINTS; EMERGENCE; MOVEMENT
AB Creativity is increasingly recognized as a key factor in team sport performance. While physical, technical, and tactical skills remain central in player evaluation, they do not fully account for athletes' ability to make relevant motor decisions in complex, uncertain situations. This article introduces a methodological framework for assessing socio-motor creativity, defined as the capacity to generate novel and appropriate motor behaviors during dynamic interactions with teammates and opponents. Grounded in the concept of praxical communication, the framework identifies three indicators of divergent creativity-fluency, flexibility, and originality-alongside a complementary convergence score based on expert judgment. These indicators are measured through an ecological video-based observation protocol using a validated system for coding praxemes. Results from several studies reveal strong correlations between divergence and convergence scores, supporting their joint relevance for identifying creative potential. The article emphasizes the importance of in situ assessment and outlines future research directions involving conative and emotional factors in creative behavior.

TI Exploring exposure to spontaneous learning and redundancy in learning at
   a chiropractic student conference in South Africa
SO JOURNAL OF CHIROPRACTIC EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chiropractic; Students; Conferences; Learning
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; TRUSTWORTHINESS
AB Objective: This study aimed to explore chiropractic students' perceptions of their learning experiences during the 2023 World Congress of Chiropractic Students African Regional Event. The focus was on identifying benefits related to spontaneous learning, assessing the impact of social and equivalence redundancy, and uncovering opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and professional development. Methods: This was a thematic qualitative, exploratory descriptive design. Chiropractic students who attended the event participated in semistructured interviews; data saturation was achieved after 12 interviews. Data were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using Tesch's 8-step coding method. Trustworthiness was ensured through Guba's 4 criteria: credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability. Results: Seven major themes emerged namely. interdisciplinary collaboration and integration, networking and knowledge exchange with fellow professionals, skill enhancement techniques and diverse practice methods, internship portfolio requirements, career pathways awareness, practical clinical application in real-world settings, and areas for enhancement and progress. Students reported gaining valuable spontaneous knowledge, including exposure to techniques not covered in their formal curriculum. However, instances of social and equivalence redundancy limited the novelty of some learning experiences. Additional concerns included limited student participation, insufficient marketing, and financial barriers to attendance. Conclusion: The conference provided experiential learning through exposure to diverse professional perspectives and practices. Comments from interviewees suggest that future student conferences should be strategically structured to address content redundancy, enhance marketing and student access, and incorporate broader interdisciplinary participation. Such improvements may better support chiropractic students' academic and professional development.

TI A Longitudinal Analysis of School Mobility for Students in Foster Care
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE At-risk students; educational policy; policy; longitudinal studies;
   regression analyses; secondary data analysis; students in foster care;
   school mobility; educational stability; school of origin
ID ACHIEVEMENT; DISRUPTION; STABILITY; GROWTH; POLICY
AB This paper uses California administrative records to examine school mobility among students in foster care. Students in foster care change schools at higher rates than their peers, with residential moves-often linked to foster care placement changes-serving as a major driver. Students typically relocate more than 20 miles, making transportation to support educational stability challenging. They are also more likely to transfer to alternative education settings, especially after subsequent moves. In some cases, students move to better-resourced schools. School mobility declined from 36% in 2017-18 to 30% in 2023-24. Although most contributing factors remained consistent over time, some community factors, such as child poverty, became more relevant after the pandemic. These findings underscore the importance of cross-sector collaboration between education and social services to better support students in foster care.

TI High Performing Pell Institutions: Identifying and Exploring Colleges
   and Universities with High Low-Income Student Success
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Correlational analysis; descriptive analysis; economic mobility;
   economics of education; equity; graduation; higher education; low-income
   students; observational research; Pell Grants; policy; prediction;
   regression analyses; secondary data analysis; social stratification
ID MOBILITY; ACCESS; TRENDS; AID
AB Higher education serves as an unequal pathway to upward mobility, where students from low-income backgrounds are less likely to enroll and earn a degree. We develop an empirical model that systematically identifies institutions across multiple measures of success at serving students from lower-income backgrounds. We identify 149 diverse "High Performing Pell" institutions, having high Pell graduation rates, low access and attainment gaps between Pell and non-Pell students, and relatively high earnings after graduation. We also show that traditional quantitative measures do a poor job of explaining this performance, underscoring how observable and unobservable factors combine to develop supportive environments for marginalized students. Our work unifies prior conceptualizations of what drives Pell recipients' outcomes and serves as an innovative approach to identify postsecondary exemplars. We provide a foundation for further multi-modal inquiry into institutions that have successfully reduced or eliminated socioeconomic attainment gaps worthy of attention by policymakers, practitioners, and funders.

TI Pharmacy students' reflections on a TED talk about difficult
   conversations
SO PHARMACY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Communication; Difficult healthcare conversation; Pharmacy student; TED
   talk
AB Background: Educating health professions students in difficult conversations is necessary, and the expanding role of pharmacists necessitates this instruction for pharmacy students. Methods: This exploratory qualitative study was modelled after a similar project with undergraduate nursing students. Second- (P2) and third year (P3) pharmacy students were invited to participate. Students watched the TED talk "On Being Present, Not Perfect" about difficult conversations and answered two reflection questions prior to a required lab course session. Student comments were categorised by a priori themes. Results: Fifty-two of 236 total students (23%) agreed to participate in the study; 36 were P2s and 16 were P3s. Treating the patient as a person was noted across each of the themes. Limitations: This study was conducted at a single, private, faith-based institution; participation was voluntary; data were self-reported; and no objective measures of communication skills were used. Conclusion: The students reflected on TED Talk about difficult conversations and the importance of treating patients with respect as a person. The reflective component encouraged students to assimilate the content along with experiences from their professional work or personal life.

Pharmacy students are particularly at risk due to their access to medications and confidence in self-prescribing. This study assessed the prevalence of antibiotic self-medication among pharmacy students at Mosul University, comparing knowledge and practices across different training stages, and explored their proposed solutions. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 382 students (187 second-year, 195 fifth-year) to assess demographics, knowledge, awareness, attitudes, and practices. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and various statistical tests. Results: A total of 80.6% of students reported self-medication in the past year, with fifth-year students showing a higher prevalence (89.7%) compared to second-year students (71.1%; p < 0.0001). Fifth-year students had greater knowledge of antibiotic effectiveness (68.7% vs. 32.6%), AMR awareness (96.9% vs. 50.8%), and adverse consequences (94.4% vs. 27.8%). Despite these differences, multivariable analysis showed that the knowledge score was not independently associated with selfmedication (p = 0.761), whereas fifth-year status remained significant (p < 0.0001). Conclusion: The findings indicate that greater knowledge is associated with higher rates of self-medication among fifth-year students. Integrating stewardship principles early in curricula, enforcing prescription-only policies, and launching collaborative awareness campaigns could address this knowledge-behaviour gap.

AB Background: Students often struggle to move from recalling guidelines to making systematic, patient-centred decisions about antimicrobials. TI Association between Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE)
   station order and clinical competence assessment in pharmacy students
SO PHARMACY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Clinical skills assessment; OSCE; Pharmacy student; Student performance
ID WORKING-MEMORY; PERFORMANCE
AB Background: Objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) are used to assess clinical skills in pharmacy education. Some concern exists regarding station order and OSCE performance, but data are lacking in pharmacy students. The purpose of this study was to determine whether OSCE station order or first-station student confidence are associated with overall OSCE performance in third-year pharmacy (P3) students. Methods: This retrospective observational cohort study included P3 students completing four three-station formative OSCEs and a two-day summative OSCE with four stations per day. Stations were ranked by difficulty using pre-determined cut scores. For formative OSCEs, students also reported immediate post-station confidence. Overall OSCE performance was compared between students completing the most difficult station first versus all others and between low and neutral-high first station student confidence groups using the Mann-Whitney test. Results: Completing the most difficult station first was not associated with overall formative or summative OSCE performance. However, students reporting low confidence on their first station had lower overall formative OSCE performance. Student confidence was higher on stations designated as most difficult. Conclusion: OSCE station order does not appear to impact overall performance, but low student confidence on the initial OSCE station may be associated with overall lower performance.

TI Gamified learning during Ramadan: Feasibility, completion metrics, and
   learner perceptions in a virtual Beers Criteria escape room among PharmD
   students
SO PHARMACY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive performance; Perceived cognitive impairment; Pharmacy
   education; Ramadan fasting; Saudi Arabia; Student engagement
ID SLEEP
AB Background: Ramadan fasting affects sleep, energy, and cognition for millions of Muslims. Healthcare education concerns include scheduling cognitive assessments during fasting. Gamified methods like virtual escape rooms involve reasoning, collaboration, and time pressure. This study assessed the feasibility and student perceptions of a virtual Beers Criteria escape room during Ramadan among fifth-year PharmD students. Methods: This study involved 122 fasting students who took part in a Geriatric Virtual Escape Room (G-VER) during the third week of Ramadan. Metrics included completion time and hints used. A survey assessed concentration, problem-solving, confidence, sleep, energy, collaboration, and engagement. Results: All students completed the activity within 90 minutes (100% rate). The average time was 32.4 +/- 3.9 minutes, with 1.45 +/- 0.95 hints used. Although 69.7% reported reduced concentration and 51.6% perceived impairment during fasting, performance remained high. Most reported moderate energy (53.3%) and found the activity more enjoyable than traditional tests (73%). Female students completed faster (p < 0.001), but males showed higher confidence (p = 0.046). Conclusion: Implementing a gamified pharmacotherapy assessment during Ramadan was feasible and well received. Many students faced cognitive challenges while fasting but completed the activity on time despite perceived strain. These findings support scheduling interactive learning during Ramadan and highlight the need to address student perceptions of cognitive strain.

TI AEED: Agentic Edge-AI Engagement Detection for K-12 Classrooms
SO IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON LEARNING TECHNOLOGIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Modeling; Labeling; Learning (artificial intelligence); Training;
   Educational institutions; Design methodology; Electroencephalography;
   Videos; Artificial intelligence; Testing; Agentic AI; classroom
   analytics; convergent research; cross-disciplinary; ECG; EEG; edge AI;
   embodied cognition; engagement detection; K-12 classrooms; physiological
   computing
ID HEART-RATE-VARIABILITY; VALUES
AB Monitoring classroom participation requires dependable, low-latency, private solutions that work within edge hardware constraints while maintaining meaningful learning connections. On-device inference is conceivable with edge-AI systems, but they rarely analyze input signal importance in real-world classroom scenarios and employ face orientation or gaze as crude proxies. The embodied cognition theory predicts that engagement should be represented in whole-body sensorimotor activity on specific tasks, not only in face configuration, but agentic classroom pipelines have not operationalized this requirement. In this article, we present agentic edge-AI engagement detection (AEED), a cross-disciplinary pipeline that leverages classroom deployment constraints to inform model design, data collection, and system development. In particular, AEED consists of BodyPosture (BP), a model trained on traditional camera-facing body-orientation cues, and FaceReaction (FR), a face model with labels derived from synchronized EEG, ECG, and task performance. In order to examine the impact of input design alongside architectural and platform characteristics, both models operate in parallel under the same tracking, hardware, and logging settings. The pipeline uses commodity edge hardware for interaction recording, dual-model inference, and anonymous student tracking. When camera geometry changes, BP's orientation-based signals invert, whereas FR's physiologically grounded signals correlate with learning outcomes in contexts similar to its training conditions. These results suggest that input design and label construction may matter more than architectural choice for deployment validity, although training-domain differences between the two models remain a partial confound. For agentic AI systems in authentic classrooms, these findings offer a reproducible framework for building embodied, per-student engagement trajectories.

TI Socioeconomic and Gender Inequalities in the Development of
   Social-Emotional Skills in Latin American Students
SO REVISTA ELECTRONICA DE INVESTIGACION EDUCATIVA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE social skills; emotional and social development; educational
   disadvantage; Latin America
AB The development of social-emotional skills is a core component of the right to a quality education, yet it continues to occupy a marginal position in policies aimed at reducing inequalities in Latin America. This study seeks to determine the impact of gender and socioeconomic status on five PISA indicators relating to the social-emotional dimension of learning in secondary school students in Latin America, while quantifying the proportion of variability attributable to schools and countries. Based on a secondary analysis of PISA 2022 microdata, multivariate multilevel models were estimated with a sample of 66,037 fifteen-year-old students from 12 Latin American countries. These findings demonstrate that educational inequalities extend beyond academic achievement and reinforce the need to expand the equity agenda to include social-emotional dimensions of learning.

AB : This study had two objectives: first, to evaluate the factor structure of the German Inventory of Callous-Unemotional Traits (ICU) in adolescence, and second, to investigate the interplay between callous-unemotional (CU) traits, aggressive behavior, and bullying perpetration in German adolescents. The sample consisted of 1,321 adolescents (55.18 % female). Confirmatory factor analyses reveal a two-factor model with callousness and uncaring. TI Breaking "Chemistry Is Boring" Stereotypes for Engineering Students
   Through the Use of Gamification
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GAME-BASED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational Escape Rooms; Educational Technology; Engineering Education;
   Chemistry Education; Learning; Engineering Degree; University
ID ESCAPE ROOM; GENERAL-CHEMISTRY; SCIENCE; COURSES; IMPACT
AB Low levels of engagement with chemistry among undergraduate engineering students have been associated with high failure and attrition rates. It seems that traditional lecture-based instruction has not aligned with Generation Z students' preference for interactive learning. This study involved the design, implementation, and evaluation of an educational escape room aimed at improving first-year engineering students' understanding of chemistry and their attitudes toward the subject at the University of M & aacute;laga, Spain. The escape room was implemented as summative assessment worth 10% of the course grade, across three engineering programs during the academic years 2018-2019 and 2022-2023. Students' perceptions were collected through a validated online questionnaire. Survey responses (n = 135) indicated high satisfaction levels. Most participants reported that the activity improved their understanding of theoretical concepts and was more engaging than traditional assessments. Overall, the results suggested that educational escape rooms, through active learning and teamwork, enhanced engagement and promoted positive attitudes toward chemistry.

TI Defining Game-Based Learning: Addressing Terminological Variations
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GAME-BASED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Games; Education; Literature Review; Systematization; Definitions
AB Game-based learning (GBL) has emerged as a widely discussed educational approach; however, this term may be referred to by various names, creating challenges for both research and practice. This article examines terminological gaps in the existing discourse on GBL and distinguishes it from related concepts such as gamification, serious games, etc. The focus is on understanding GBL and the related terminology provided. For this reason, a systematic literature analysis of 52 articles was conducted. Key findings contain an overview of the definition of "game-based learning" and its 72 variations. To gain a better understanding, terms were analyzed to answer the following questions: what specific characteristics are mentioned in its definition, what purpose it serves, and where it is most frequently used. A possible definition based on the common understanding of what GBL entails was proposed.

TI Sex-Based Differences in Recreational Modern Board Gaming in Spain:
   Implications for Board Game-Based Learning
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GAME-BASED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Board Game-Based Learning; Modern Board Games; Sex Differences; Player
   Profiles; Facilitation; Inclusive Learning Environments
ID TIME; PLAY
AB This cross-sectional study examined sex-based differences in recreational modern board gaming in Spain and their relevance to inclusive board game-based learning. A total of 1,090 participants aged 10-86 completed an online survey; inferential analyses compared 446 men and 634 women. Women reported earlier, more family-based entry into board gaming, whereas men more often entered through friends. Men reported more frequent and longer play, greater event attendance, larger collections, greater use of specialized media and platforms, greater self-perceived confidence in game mechanics, and more solo play. After adjustment for age and education, men had higher odds of BoardGameGeek/ LaBSK registration and event attendance and were more likely to be classified as Type II/Facilitators or Type III/Specialists. Although classroom behavior and learning outcomes were not assessed, the findings suggest unequal experiential starting points that educators should consider when scaffolding rules, rotating facilitation roles, and designing equitable board game-based learning environments.

TI Board Game-Based Learning for Music Notation
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GAME-BASED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Analog Tabletop Activities; Instructional Design; Lower Secondary
   Education; Student Engagement; Achievement Testing; Teacher Debriefing;
   Peer Interaction; Classroom Evaluation
ID EMPIRICAL-EVIDENCE; COMPUTER GAMES; SERIOUS GAMES; GAMIFICATION;
   METAANALYSIS
AB This article presents a classroom design evaluation of a teacher-guided analog tabletop instructional sequence for basic music notation practice. The intervention, Adventure in the Land of Magical Notes, consisted of three sequential tabletop activities targeting note recognition, staff positions, note values, and rests. Thirty-two Grade 7 students participated in a 12-period sequence that combined teacher briefing, small-group play, answer checking, feedback, debriefing, and evaluation. Developmental pilot tests with non-sample students indicated that the materials met the 80/80 instructional-efficiency benchmark used in Thai educational media development practice (80.39/81.17). In the main classroom sample, posttest scores on a 40-item notation test were higher than pretest scores, and satisfaction ratings were high. Because the study used a single-group pretest-posttest design, findings are interpreted as preliminary within-group classroom evidence rather than causal evidence of effectiveness. The article offers a design case for aligning tabletop mechanics with classroom notation tasks.

TI Is This Still Medical Education? The Educational Use of Nude Pediatric
   Clinical Photographs: Bioethical Reassessment
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE medical education; clinical photography; pediatric patients; bioethics;
   educational value; educational accountability; educational; necessity;
   visual ethics; clinical images; medical publishing
ID COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY; GUIDELINES; DERMATOLOGY; PRINCIPLES; ACCEPTANCE;
   PERCEPTION; CONSENT
AB Clinical photography can convey phenotypic, anatomical, and diagnostic information that may be difficult to replace with text. This also applies to highly sensitive pediatric clinical photographs when the scope of patient exposure is necessary to achieve a specific educational objective. This viewpoint addresses a more specific problem: "How should the educational function of a highly sensitive pediatric clinical photograph be evaluated when the condition identified with the photograph is substantively described elsewhere in the educational material?" The analysis is grounded in a documented longitudinal observation of 28 editions and reprints of a single academic textbook lineage published between 2005 and 2019, across which the same image-condition configuration persisted. At the point of image presentation, the depicted clinical conditions were explicitly identified, while the accompanying text stated that they were described elsewhere in the textbook, where their substantive clinical descriptions were located in accordance with the textbook's declared curricular structure. On this basis, I propose educational disconnection to describe a situation in which the image-specific educational contribution at the point of presentation is difficult to reconstruct from the observable relationship among image location, the clinical condition identified with the image, the condition's declared curricular location, the location of its substantive clinical description, and the destination indicated in the text accompanying the photograph. The central distinction is that identification of a clinical condition, identification of where that condition is substantively described, and identification of the educational contribution of its photograph are not the same. A separate question therefore remains: "What additional educational information does the image contribute here?" The longitudinal dimension extends this analysis through the concept of educational value decay, referring to the possibility that the relationship between an image and the context-specific justification for its presence may weaken over time, without assuming that educational value automatically declines with the age or repeated reproduction of the image. In response, I propose an Educational Reassessment Framework-a practical, event-triggered process that proceeds from identifying the image's educational function and its relationship to the curricular structure, through assessment of its image-specific educational contribution and exposure-function proportionality, to the consideration of equivalent alternatives, the continuing validity of its justification, and the conditions of responsible continued use. Reassessment is not intended to automatically remove historical, repeatedly used, or highly sensitive photographs. Responsible reuse of an educationally valuable image may remain justified and may reduce the need to photograph additional patients, but educational value does not substitute for appropriate authorization or other conditions of responsible use. Its purpose is to determine whether continued use is supported by an identifiable, current, and context-specific educational contribution, whether the scope of patient information disclosed is necessary and proportionate to that contribution, and whether the conditions supporting use remain appropriate.

TI The AWARE (AI Use, Why, Attachment, Reality and Risk, and Effect on
   Functioning) Framework for Assessing Patients' Use of AI in Mental
   Health Care
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; AI; conversational artificial intelligence;
   large language models; ChatGPT; psychiatry; mental health; psychiatric
   interview; clinical assessment; medical education; digital mental health
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE
AB Conversational AI has rapidly become integrated into everyday life, with many individuals using large language model-based systems, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, for education, productivity, health information, decision-making, emotional support, and companionship. As patients increasingly incorporate conversational AI into their cognitive, emotional, and social lives, these interactions may influence coping strategies, treatment engagement, clinical decision-making, and mental health outcomes. However, although medical education has increasinglyemphasizedAI literacy and the responsibleuse ofgenerative AI by clinicians, comparatively little attention has been given to preparing health care professionals to assess patients' use of conversational AI during routine clinical encounters. This Viewpoint introduces the AWARE (AI use, why, attachment, reality and risk, and effecton functioning) framework, a practical educational framework designed to help mental health professionals systematically assess patients' use of conversational AI. Rather than functioning as a diagnostic instrument or psychometric scale, AWARE provides a structured approach to psychiatric interviewing across 5 clinically relevant domains: AI use, why, attachment, reality and risk, and effect on functioning. Together, these domains guide clinicians in exploring patterns of AI use, the motivations underlying engagement, the emotional significance of patient-AI interactions, potential influences on reality testing and clinical risk, and the overall impact of AI on psychological well-being, daily functioning, relationships, and recovery. The framework is intended to complement existing psychiatric interviewing practices by supporting comprehensive history taking, clinical reasoning, risk assessment, documentation, and learner education. We discuss the rationale for routinely asking patients about AI use, review emerging evidence regarding both the potential benefits and risks of conversational AI, and describe how AWARE may be incorporated into undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing professional education through simulation, objective structured clinical examinations, workplace-based assessment, and clinical supervision. We also outline priorities for future research, including validation, implementation, educational evaluation, and cross-cultural adaptation. As conversational AI becomes increasingly embedded within patients' daily lives, clinicians require practical approaches to understanding its role in mental health and health care. The AWARE framework offers a structured educational starting point for integrating assessment of patient-AI interactions into routine psychiatric interviewing while supporting patient-centered, evidence-informed clinical practice and health professions education.

TI Students' Learning Outcomes in a Virtual Microscopic Online and
   Face-to-Face Anatomy Course: Cross-Over Comparative Study
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE virtual slides; hybrid course; learning outcomes; demographics; blended
   learning
ID TECHNOLOGY; HISTOLOGY; LESSONS
AB Background: Since 2021, the histology of organs in the microscopic anatomy course at the Department of Anatomy II of the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universit & auml;t Munich has been held as a hybrid course using a 3D virtual microscopy system. Evidence comparing synchronous online versus face-to-face instruction using an advanced 3D virtual slide system remains limited. In particular, it is unclear whether learning outcomes are equivalent across instructional modes, and whether individual student characteristics influence learning outcomes under these conditions. Objective: This study systematically (1) compares the learning outcomes of preclinic students attending a microscopic anatomy course either face-to-face or synchronously online using a 3D virtual microscopy slide box generated from fully scanned histological glass slides previously used in a traditional course, and (2) investigates whether selected demographic characteristics and personal skills predict learning outcomes in either instructional mode. We hypothesized that learning outcomes would not differ between online and face-to-face participation when instructional conditions are identical. Methods: The students attended 2 consecutive course days on 2 topics (kidney and liver) in a crossover design. Half of the students attended the first day face-to-face, and the second day online, while the other half attended in the reverse order. Demographic characteristics (eg, self-organization and affinity for technology interaction) and learning outcomes were collected via survey and simulated examination on the day after the second course day. To minimize potential confounding factors (eg, learning by means of external resources) and to ensure that the results reflected the learning outcomes within the scope of this study, 2 particularly challenging course days were intentionally selected, and the time interval before the simulated examination was kept short. Learning outcomes were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model, and potential predictors were explored using stepwise linear regression. Results: Overall, 740 student questionnaires and examinations (740/864, 86% of the total student cohort) were used to assess the items' quality of the simulated examination. Inferential analyses included data from 415 students who completed the crossover design as intended. No significant main effect of participation mode on learning outcomes was found (F-1,F- 413=0.16; P=.69). Although a significant effect of examination topic was observed (F-1,F- 413=25.56; P<.001), there was no significant interaction between participation mode and examination topic (F-1,F- 413=0.13; P=.72). Regression analyses showed low predictive power overall (R-2 >= 0.12), with self-organization emerging as a weak but consistent predictor across both instructional modes. Conclusions: The results of this study suggest that the microscopic anatomy learning outcomes of students under controlled short-term conditions are comparable in synchronous online and face-to-face teaching. However, it should be noted that the study was limited to 2 topics and 2 consecutive course days. Further research should address additional topics, long-term learning outcomes, and broader student populations.

TI Quality is not enough: the 'Social Override' effect and the primacy of
   hedonic motivation in Gen Z's EdTech adoption
SO RESEARCH IN LEARNING TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE mobile-assisted language learning; peer influence; technology adoption;
   collectivist culture; Vietnam
ID ACCEPTANCE
AB What drives Generation Z (Gen Z) university students in Vietnam to adopt and keep using Mobile English Learning Apps: content quality or something else? This study proposes a Social Override effect, that is, a pattern in which peer validation and hedonic engagement, rather than content quality, appear to drive actual use even when information quality is adequate. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, this study analysed survey data from 150 Vietnamese university students alongside 10 semi-structured interviews. Information Quality did not significantly predict actual use (beta = 0.147, p = 0.103); Hedonic Motivation did (beta = 0.401, p < 0.001). This pattern is consistent with a hygiene-factor interpretation of content quality: its absence may generate dissatisfaction, but its presence does not, on its own, increase usage. The interviews help explain why. In this setting, peer recommendation and group-based app use create a buffer that lets students overlook technical limitations and advertising friction. Among these Gen Z students, trust was expressed through interface aesthetics and social visibility more than through content accuracy. Whether the same pattern holds beyond Vietnamese university students is a question this single study cannot settle.

TI The Equity Paradox in Disadvantaged High Schools in Chile
SO REVISTA ELECTRONICA DE INVESTIGACION EDUCATIVA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE educational discrimination; social justice; educational interactions
   processes; educational policy
ID POLICY
AB Educational policies play a key role in promoting equity worldwide. However, various studies have argued that these policies do not always achieve their intended outcomes. The objective of this research was to explore how administrative and management teams in socioeconomically disadvantaged high schools interpret and translate educational policies aimed at promoting equity, in addition to the potential challenges for developing quality teaching-learning processes. The study was exploratory and employed a qualitative, crosssectional design, with a critical sociological approach. Interviews were conducted with 16 members of leadership and management teams from four socioeconomically disadvantaged secondary schools in the Valparaiso Region, Chile. Thematic analysis was used to process the information. The main findings indicate that equity policies are interpreted and implemented in a partial manner and from a deficit perspective that permeates school life, helping to shape inequitable teaching-learning processes that reinforce and perpetuate social inequalities. This study sounds the alarm about a paradox of equity policies in education and discusses the critical impact this has both on teaching-learning processes and on the student-teacher relationship.
