TI VISIONARA-developing a concept for decentralized competency-based
   learning in primary health care and its proposed evaluation
SO GMS JOURNAL FOR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate medical education; primary health care; competency-based
   education; general practice education; family practice education;
   clinical clerkship; curriculum; teaching
ID COMPLEX INTERVENTIONS; CLINICIAN-EDUCATOR; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; COMMUNITY;
   STUDENTS; PROGRAM; PERFORMANCE; DOCTORS
AB Background: To educate high-quality medical graduates who can contribute to a resilient, primary care-based health system, medical education must shift its focus towards decentralized and curricular competency-based medical education (CBME). However, undergraduate general practice education in Germany remains fragmented: theoretical content is delivered at universities, while practical experience is confined to clerkships in community practices, which often lack sufficient didactic infrastructure. This persistent separation of theory and practice hinders the genuine transformation towards CBME. New models that embed structured teaching directly within real care environments are required to bridge this gap. Approach: VISIOn Network of Academic Reference Practices in General Medicine (VISIONARA) introduces a novel model for decentralized competency-oriented education in general practice. By establishing academic teaching clusters within community practices, the program creates structured, contextually anchored learning environments that enable experiential learning and professional development. While the initiative aligns with the Medical Research Council (MRC) framework for complex interventions, its primary innovation lies in its design as a scalable model for competency-based learning integrated directly into real-world practice. Methods: Following the Medical Research Council (MRC) framework, this paper reports on the first two phases: (1) concept development and (2) pilot planning. The development phase comprised a synthesis of evidence on competency-based and decentralized medical education, design of a didactic model based on Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, and process/outcome modelling to guide feasibility testing. The pilot phase will assess the model's feasibility, acceptability, and integration into routine general practice. Discussion: VISIONARA seeks to bridge the gap between theoretical academic instruction and real-world healthcare in general practice education by embedding structured, competency-based learning within authentic clinical settings. The feasibility study will examine financial and personnel resource requirements, acceptance among practice staff, students, and patients. It will further assess organizational integration into routine practice workflows, and the identification of structural and logistical barriers. These findings will inform further refinement and the potential progression to a subsequent evaluation phase.

TI Understanding of medical leadership from the perspective of medical
   students at the start of their studies and in their final year - a
   qualitative focus group study
SO GMS JOURNAL FOR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE leadership; competence; medical studies; professional identity
ID TRANSACTIONAL LEADERSHIP; CHARISMATIC LEADERSHIP; MANAGEMENT
AB Background: Physicians have to take on a wide range of leadership responsibilities, management as well as leadership tasks. A purely management-orientated approach is no longer sufficient to be successful as a physician leader in the dynamic healthcare sector. This explorative, qualitative study therefore analyzed the understanding of medical leadership among students in their first-semester and in their final year. Methods: Seven group discussions were conducted with 14 first-semester and 17 final-year students, participating in homogenous cohorts. These group discussions were transcribed verbatim, analyzed using Kuckartz' content-structuring qualitative content analysis, and compared with international frameworks. Results: A total of 514 text segments were coded which could be assigned to 12 main categories comprising 49 subcategories. The main category "Demonstrating emotional-social competence" was the most frequently mentioned in both cohorts. Differences emerged between the cohorts regarding the perspectives on personnel development though. While first-semester students emphasized the development of the leaders themselves, final-year students discussed the development of the employees more frequently. Not all aspects of the international frameworks became visible in the students' understanding. Conclusion: Medical students showed a relatively comprehensive understanding of medical leadership, but not all aspects of recognized frameworks were included in their understanding. Since a cohort-specific perspective on some aspects of medical leadership emerged, this varying need for development could be addressed by a longitudinal curriculum on medical leadership.

TI FamuPlus - a pilot project to support self-oriented learning through
   self-created learning outcomes in clinical electives
SO GMS JOURNAL FOR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE self-oriented learning; clinical electives; learning outcomes; SMART
   criteria; medical education; project implementation
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; SMART
AB Background: Clinical electives in German medical education provide valuable insights into healthcare practice but often lack structured learning guidance. The FamuPlus project was developed to support medical students in defining and pursuing self-created learning outcomes to foster self-oriented learning (SOL), which is recognized as a key competence for lifelong learning and professional development in medical practice. In this study, self-created learning outcomes describe a guided process. Project description: Within FamuPlus, seven students completed a brief online training introducing the SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound) framework and the learning domains of Bloom's taxonomy. Thereafter, participants formulated individual learning outcomes prior to their clinical elective and reviewed them with their clinical teachers (e.g. general practitioner or ward physician, etc.) at the beginning of their independently chosen, monthlong, clinical elective on site. Throughout the elective, students reflected on their progress using an online self-evaluation tool and engaged in guided follow-up discussions about their experiences. To evaluate the intervention, a control group was additionally surveyed at the end of the clinical elective. Results and experiences: Students reported that defining their own learning outcomes improved focus, motivation, and perceived learning success it also seemed to promote self-efficacy during their electives. However, designing measurable learning outcomes was challenging. Discussion and conclusion: FamuPlus appears to be a feasible approach to support medical students in strengthening SOL during clinical electives. Despite the small, potentially highly motivated cohort the findings suggest beneficial effects of FamuPlus on perceived learning success, motivation and focus. Refinement and broader implementation are warranted to strengthen learner-centred education in clinical electives. The low-threshold online format and minimal faculty workload make the approach transferable to other faculties. For widespread implementation, careful consideration should be given to the involvement of faculty staff, depending on the available resources as adequate infrastructure is essential for sustainable implementation.

TI From competency mapping to curriculum development: Identifying gaps in
   an undergraduate general practice clerkship-a mixed-methods study
SO GMS JOURNAL FOR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate medical education; competency-based education; general
   practice; family practice; clinical clerkship; curriculum; medical
   schools/organization & administration; teaching
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES; SPECIALTY CHOICE; STUDENT;
   SCHOOL; MODEL
AB Objectives: This study aims to show the process of developing a competency-based medical education (CBME) General Practice (GP) block clerkship at the University of Heidelberg, aligned with frameworks such as CanMEDS, Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs), and the National Competency-based Learning Objectives Catalogue (NKLM 2.0). Objectives are to identify competencies addressed in the current two-week clerkship, determine additional content needed to cover all required competencies, and assess student perspectives. Methods: A questionnaire completed by 165 students in 2023 evaluated perceived competence in various areas and their interest in GP before and after the clerkship. Data were analysed using a 5-point Likert scale ((1=fully agree to 5=completely disagree), and the curriculum was mapped to NKLM 2.0, CanMEDS, and EPAs to identify represented and missing competencies. Focus group meetings with lecturers and students were held to develop a new concept. Results: The current clerkship received an overall rating of 1.8 (SD: 1.06) but did not significantly increase interest in GP careers. Some competencies were well-covered, but areas like interprofessional skills or leadership and management were lacking. A six-week longitudinal clerkship was proposed to address these gaps, focusing on interprofessional collaboration, leadership, and patient-centred care, and including digital teaching, reflection and simulation training, and shadowing experiences. Conclusion: The proposed CBME curriculum addresses evolving needs in medical education. Successful implementation will require longitudinal integration, interdisciplinary cooperation, trained preceptors, and centralised coordination. This study provides a roadmap for emphasising key competencies, promoting GP career choice, and contributing to high-quality patient care.

TI AI-based virtual patient interactions improve professional language
   proficiency in international nurses
SO GMS JOURNAL FOR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE international healthcare personnel; professional language training;
   nursing education; virtual interaction training; virtual patients
ID BARRIERS
AB Objectives: International healthcare personnel face significant challenges in language acquisition. We investigated whether virtual patient interaction (VI) training can support professional integration and clinical language proficiency. Methods: In an explorative controlled study, 25 international nursing staff undergoing professional qualification measures in Germany were included. The intervention group (n=13) received access to casuu, a digital simulation tool providing interactive communication scenarios with virtual patients and colleagues. The control group (n=12) followed standard language training without VI. Both groups received 600 hours of training for the B2 for Nursing exam, as required for professional licensure in several German states, at the same language school using the same textbook. The primary outcome was the fail rate at the first attempt, with effects on different skill dimensions assessed in addition. The clinical supervisors were interviewed 12-14 months after the arrival. Results: The fail rate in the B2 for Nursing exam was reduced from 66.7% in the control group to 25.0% in the intervention group (relative reduction 62.5%). Competence increased primarily in the skill dimension "active speaking". Attrition rates did not increase (1/13 vs. 2/12). Clinical superiors reported increased confidence and competence in team and patient interactions in the intervention group. Conclusion: Virtual interaction-based training improves the acquisition of professional language and clinical communication skills of international nurses. It integrates with conventional teaching and does not increase dropout rates.

TI The CBHPE Outcomes Theory of Change: An International Consensus
   Statement on the Mechanisms and Outcomes of Competency-Based Education
   in the Health Professions
SO PERSPECTIVES ON MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; IMPLEMENTATION; MODEL; ACQUISITION; LEARNER; DESIGN;
   TIME
AB Introduction: Competency-Based Health Professions Education (CBHPE) is an outcomes-based approach to planning and conceptualizing the training of health professionals to serve population needs. Despite its uptake, ongoing debate persists regarding the assumptions underpinning CBHPE, its intended purposes, and how success should be defined and evaluated. This contributes to variable implementation and difficulty aligning core features with meaningful outcomes. To date, no published theory of change has articulated how CBHPE's core components provide a framework for later evaluation of intended outcomes. Methods: Using Funnell and Rogers' purposeful program theory, the authors, all members of the International Competency-based Education Health Professions Educators Collaborative (ICBHPE), developed a model theory of change. The authors conducted a broad review of CBHPE literature, supplemented by CBE frameworks from adjacent educational contexts to strengthen underdeveloped constructs in implementation and evaluation. Findings were iteratively synthesized into a program theory and refined through repeated cycles of large-group feedback, consensus building, and member checking within ICBHPE. Results: The authors developed a CBHPE Outcomes Theory of Change that articulates key assumptions, mechanisms of impact, and expected outcomes associated with CBHPE implementation. The framework specifies how van Melle's CBHPE core components are theorized to function across phases of implementation and identifies proximal and distal outcomes that can reasonably be expected, based on intentional, deliberate program evaluation at each implementation and evaluation stage. Discussion: The CBHPE Outcomes Theory of Change offers scholars and implementers a practical guide to enhance the quality and fidelity of implementation, evaluation, and research efforts related to CBHPE worldwide. Using this guide as a framework, programs can plan, implement, and then examine whether the intended outcomes of CBHPE have been realized.

TI Responsible Artificial Intelligence Integration in Medical Student
   Education in Somalia and Low-Resource Settings: A Context-Sensitive
   Implementation Framework
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; clinical reasoning; academic
   integrity; virtual patients; faculty development; digital equity
AB Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI and large language models, is increasingly used by health-professions learners for explanation, revision, simulation, feedback, and assessment support, while institutional governance has not always kept pace. Somalia is a distinctive setting in which recent mapping identified 112 health-professions schools, many concentrated in urban areas, while medical education continues to face unequal access to faculty, simulation, standardized assessment, and reliable digital infrastructure. This commentary proposes a context-sensitive implementation framework for responsible AI integration in medical student education in Somalia and comparable low-resource settings. The framework was developed through a focused narrative synthesis of Somalia-specific educational evidence, peer-reviewed AI-in-medical-education literature, and international guidance from WHO, UNESCO, and the Association of American Medical Colleges. Its contribution is to translate broad AI principles into a resource-constrained implementation pathway that links Somalia-specific educational constraints to defined AI-supported functions, governance safeguards, phased institutional actions, and measurable educational outcomes. Published studies support the feasibility of AI-assisted feedback, virtual patient simulation, and tutoring, but also demonstrate variable accuracy and the need for human verification. The proposed model therefore prioritizes faculty oversight, academic integrity, patient confidentiality, multilingual verification, local clinical validation, low-bandwidth access, and outcome monitoring. A phased roadmap moves from policy and lowrisk pilots to curriculum integration and multi-institutional evaluation. The framework is conceptual and requires prospective validation. If implemented with simultaneous investment in faculty development and assessment reform, AI may expand access to supervised practice without replacing teachers, patients, bedside learning, or professional judgment.

TI Navigating Global Education: Students' Perception of a Transcontinental
   COIL
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE collaborative online international learning; COIL; green pedagogy;
   intercultural competence; global citizenship; digital literacy
AB Introduction: This study explores students' perceptions of a transcontinental Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) project involving participants from Brazil, Ireland, the Philippines, South Africa, and Spain. Leveraging principles of green pedagogy and intercultural collaboration, the virtual exchange (VEX) was designed to cultivate disciplinary knowledge, professional skills, intercultural awareness, and digital literacy, ultimately fostering global citizenship. Methods: This was an exploratory mixed-methods study, that combined quantitative survey data on student-lecturer engagement, vocational skills development, cultural diversity, and digital learning platforms, alongside qualitative insights from semi-structured interviews. Results: Our findings highlight how the VEX enriched professional learning, critical analysis abilities, and cross-cultural understanding while supporting networking and collaborative research across five time zones. During this time, COVID-19 posed challenges to higher education, however, it also served as a catalyst for accelerating international virtual collaboration and digital pedagogies. Despite variations in technology access and language proficiency, the experience fostered unity, empathy, and resilience. Conclusion: The findings should be interpreted as exploratory and perception-based rather than evidence of confirmed educational impact. This study contributes to the growing body of research on COIL by providing empirical insight into how students experience transcontinental virtual collaboration in health education contexts.

TI Unpacking Factors Affecting Medical Students Engagement in Educational
   Activities at University: A Mixed-Method Study
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE motivation; factors; engagement; students; educational activities
ID FOCUS GROUP; PARTICIPATION; MOTIVATION; CLASSROOM; AUTONOMY
AB Introduction: A key component of engaging students in educational activities is identifying the factors that influence their motivation. This practice is particularly useful given the crucial role the educational system plays in student support. Methods and Materials: This multi-phase mixed-methods study in Tehran University of Medical Sciences consisted of three sequential phases: In the first phase, a literature review was conducted to identify factors reported in the literature that affect student involvement in university educational programs. In the second phase, a focus group discussion was carried out with 10 health professions students to learn about students' views and the motivating factors affecting them. In the third phase, a three-round modified Delphi study was conducted among health professions students at TUMS to determine which of the identified factors met the a priori >= 4 inclusion threshold. In this phase, 45 students take part in round 1. 41 and 39 students took part in round 2 and 3. Results: Based on the extracted codes from the focus group meeting and the first round of Delphi, the factors were categorized into five areas: "Providing opportunities for gaining personal and professional benefits", "Providing opportunities for encouragement and appreciation", "Providing opportunities for collaboration and receiving support", "Providing opportunities for personal and professional development" and "having a sense of interest, autonomy, and usefulness". In the second Delphi round out of different domains, "feeling useful" was rated as the most important motivational factor, followed by "impacting the future career" and "having the opportunity to learn and strengthen the acquisition of skills", while "gaining fame" and "availability of educational materials" received the lowest ratings. In the third round, 73% of participants agreed with the final list of motivational factors without modification. Conclusion: One of the most important responsibilities of health professions education institutions is motivating students during the educational process through the identification of proper motivational factors. Our results can offer a guide to educational policymakers and administrators.

TI Social Accountability in Medical Student Scholarly Projects: A Call for
   Intentional Integration
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE social accountability; medical students; undergraduate research;
   community engagement
ID PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT; EDUCATION; HEALTH; SCHOOL; PATIENT; CANADA; IMPACT
AB Background: While social accountability is integrated into clinical training at many institutions, its role in medical scholarly projects remains unexplored. While much has been studied on social accountability in medical education and service, little is known about how it is approached in research. Therefore, we examined whether community partnerships were included in student plans, the community's role in the research process, and health equity outcomes as measures of social accountability. Methods: We approached this observational study in two stages. In stage 1, we reviewed medical student research proposals. In stage 2, students self-identified where their projects fell on a social accountability spectrum. Results: In stage 1, we reviewed all 75 proposals submitted by the graduating class of 2025, which revealed that most student project plans lacked community involvement and that most scholarly work did not contribute to improving health equity or was not expected to. We determined that 84% (N = 63) of medical scholarly work fell outside the realm of social accountability. Fifty-seven students (N=57 of 414 total students, 14%) responded to the voluntary survey in Stage 2, recruited via a QR code embedded in the mandatory final project form. There was a shift in project self-classification after definitions of social responsiveness, social responsibility, and social accountability were provided. Respondents identified strategies to enhance accountability; however, the majority did not plan to implement these changes. Conclusion: Most scholarly projects by medical students reviewed lacked meaningful community engagement and measurable contributions to health equity. Students demonstrated improved understanding of social accountability when definitions were explicitly provided, yet the majority did not plan to act on identified strategies. These findings reveal a critical gap between institutional commitment to social accountability and its integration into student research, underscoring the need for intentional curricular interventions and structured mentorship in socially accountable research practices.

TI INTEGRATING PEER SCAFFOLDING INTO GUIDED INQUIRY LEARNING TO ENHANCE
   SCIENTIFIC LITERACY AND CRITICAL THINKING AMONG PRE-SERVICE ELEMENTARY
   SCHOOL TEACHERS

LA English
DT Article
DE guided inquiry learning; peer scaffolding; scientific literacy; critical
   thinking; pre-service elementary school teachers; science learning
ID SCIENCE-EDUCATION; ACHIEVEMENT; EXPERIENCES
AB Developing scientific literacy and critical thinking is fundamental to contemporary science education. This study explored whether integrating guided inquiry learning with peer scaffolding could improve the scientific literacy and critical thinking of pre-service elementary school teachers. A total of 226 pre-service elementary school teachers enrolled in the Basic Concepts of Elementary Science course participated in this quasi-experimental study using a pretest-posttest control group design. Students in the experimental group engaged in guided inquiry integrated with peer scaffolding, whereas the control group received conventional teaching. Peer scaffolding was systematically incorporated throughoutall phases of guided inquiry and was preceded by a pre-peer scaffolding phase involving briefing and concept reinforcement. Scientific literacy and critical thinking were assessed using validated instruments developed from the OECD/ PISA framework and Ennis'critical thinking indicators (Cronbach's alpha = .835). Data were examined using the Mann-Whitney U test, N-gain analysis, and effect size. The experimental group demonstrated significantly higher scientific literacy and critical thinking than the control group (p < .001), with N-gain scores of .676 and .773, respectively. The findings indicate that integrating peerscaffolding into guided inquiry is an effective approach for enhancing the scientific literacy and critical thinking of pre-service elementary school teachers.

TI Classification of Copper Nanoparticles Using Recovery, Optical
   Properties, and Structural Analysis

DE copper nanoparticles; laboratory interpretation; localized surface

ID SIZE
AB The process of copper nanoparticle synthesis provides undergraduates with a challenging case study for identifying materials since the relationship between copper recovery and metallic nanoparticles does not guarantee their interchangeability. Copper nanoparticle recovery may not have a pronounced plasmonic activity, and vice versa, a visually convincing colloidal solution will not necessarily provide enough information to justify a material claim. Three laboratory records of copper nanoparticle synthesis are analyzed by taking into account such parameters as reaction conditions, argon protection, optical characteristics, copper-ammonia concentrations, percent yields, particle size, and x-ray diffraction as different evidence streams and not just one pass or fail result. The laboratory record includes a pronounced optical maximum at 590 nm, the average particle diameter of 15.4 +/- 3.4 nm, face-centered cubic copper peaks at about 43.35 degrees, 50.49 degrees, 74.20 degrees, and 89.98 degrees, the copper-ammonia calibration curve slope of 42.7 M-1 cm-1 with R2 = 0.999, and three pairs of concentration and yield values of 18.4 mM/28.0%, 9.0 mM/13.5%, and 15.8 mM/23.5%. The research question poses the following query: What material-identity claims are justifiable in the cases when copper recovery, plasmonic activity, structural support, and preparation conditions are not evidentially equivalent? The research leads to the following conclusions: Sample 1 confirms a high confidence identification of metallic copper nanoparticles; Sample 2 confirms the presence of copper without metal nanoparticle identity; and Sample 3 confirms a divergence claim with reservations. The analysis demonstrates how an undergraduate experiment can help understand the importance of proper chemical interpretation of nanomaterial evidence obtained from the described synthesis, spectroscopic, colorimetric, microscopic, and diffraction measurements.

TI Resonance and Joy: A Pedagogical Relationship
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB The world we currently experience is characterized by acceleration and change. Western ideals of individualistic success, along with surrounding social structures, leads to alienation (Rosa, 2019). The purpose of education is to prepare students for the world they will encounter, but what world? We argue that rather than preparing students for a disconnected world focused on the individual, instead we aim for students to contribute to a changing future with a foundation of resilience, belonging, and connection. Hartmut Rosa (2019) has proposed the concept of resonance as a counterpoint to alienation-as an alert and present willingness to enter dialogue with the world. This view of presence has relevance to pedagogy through joy: joy becomes essential for resilience in an alienating age. This essay explores how Rosa's concept of resonance can provide a conceptual architecture for a joy-centred pedagogy. Drawing on Ross Gay's work on joy and its interaction with Rosa, we suggest that resonant pedagogical encounters create a reciprocal relationship with joy: an emergent quality of relational, dialogical, and meaningful engagements. We argue that resonance-oriented learning environments can foster the capacities students need for an uncertain future by developing attitudes, relational sensitivity, curiosity, and agency.

SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING

AB Joy-centred pedagogy is often dismissed as an "add-on" to serious teaching; however, in deficit-driven policy climates, educators increasingly describe schooling as scripted, dehumanizing, and joyless. TI Interdisciplinarity and the Epistemic Conditions of Pedagogical Joy
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB Joy-centred pedagogy has gained recent traction as educators seek alternatives to cynicism, disengagement, and burnout. Yet much of the existing discourse considers joy as an affective or motivational outcome rather than a condition grounded in epistemology. This paper offers a theoretical analysis of joy-centred pedagogy through a lens of interdisciplinarity in education (Babich, 2020), positioning interdisciplinarity not as a curricular arrangement but as an epistemological orientation that resists the fragmentation and proceduralization of knowledge common in modern educational systems. By synthesizing interdisciplinarity and joy-centred pedagogy, this paper reframes joy as an outcome of epistemic coherence and agentic engagement. Furthermore, this analysis provides a grounding of joycentred pedagogy as a theory of knowledge that supports educational vigour, care, and resilience by positioning interdisciplinarity as a foundational condition for cultivating joyful learning communities in hard times.

   Joy-Centred Pedagogical Practice

AB This conceptual article explores joy as a relational and pedagogical force in higher education, examining its connection to student motivation, well-being, and belonging through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). TI Exploring Joy Through Co-Creation: Reflections on Student-Led Course
   Design
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB Joy in higher education is often treated as incidental, yet it can be intentionally cultivated through the design of the learning environment, particularly via student-faculty co-creation. Drawing on a redesigned undergraduate positive psychology course, this work examines how involving students as partners in shaping the syllabus, assessments, and participation structures transforms the classroom's emotional and intellectual climate. Rather than framing joy as entertainment or ease, it is conceptualized as relational and emergent, arising through agency, trust, shared responsibility, and productive struggle. Four key conditions supporting the emergence of joy are identified: consequential voice, shared responsibility, relational trust, and engagement through difficulty. Evidence from both student and instructor reflections illustrates how co-creation shifts learning from compliance to commitment and from isolation to community. While tensions remain, co-creation is presented as a practical and adaptable pedagogical framework. Joy, in this context, becomes a renewable resource that signals meaningful engagement and underscores the need to rethink classroom structures in response to student disengagement and faculty burnout.

TI The Delightful Unessay: How Learners' Freedom to Choose an Assessment
   Modality Sparks Pedagogical Joy (Even in the Age of AI)
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB In this article, I argue that one of the principle ways that unessay assignments bring joy to college educators is by creating opportunities for us to work with students who are creatively and meaningfully engaging in our course content-the research fields and disciplinary tools of our own scholarly passions-using an assessment modality of their own choice. After an overview of what an unessay assignment entails, I describe how it facilitates unlearning passivity for students and unlearning didactic teaching and the transmission model of education for faculty. The unessay creates more freedom for learners to explore their own unique ideas and to find personally relevant meaning in an academic subject, making teaching with unessays an intellectually and pedagogically rewarding, even joyful, task for professors-something we all need more of in "the age of AI."

TI I Stopped Managing Students and Started Facilitating Humans:
   Recalibrating Teaching in Higher Education
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB This reflective practitioner essay examines joy-centred pedagogy as a shift from classroom management to human facilitation in higher education. Drawing on practitioner experience in performing arts teacher education and scholarship on student development, self-determination theory, and joy-centred pedagogy, it explores the limits of control-oriented approaches when working with emerging adult learners. Rather than responding to disengagement, inconsistency, or uncertainty with tighter regulation, the essay argues for joy-centred facilitation as a pedagogical stance grounded in relational clarity, shared responsibility, reflection, and intellectual risk-taking. Guided by the principle "if you don't bend, you'll break," the essay traces how one practitioner-scholar recalibrated teaching practices by moving from enforcement to dialogue, from compliance to participation, and from depleting rigour to academic vigour. Joy is framed not as ease, charisma, or positivity, but as a sustaining pedagogical resource that emerges when students are supported in struggling, revising, questioning, and growing together. Ultimately, the essay argues that sustainable, humanizing pedagogy requires educators to practice responsiveness, reconsider authority, and facilitate the humans in the room.

TI The Joy of Authenticity in the College Composition Classroom in the Age
   of AI
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB Many conversations about generative AI in the classroom often demonstrate a deficit mindset toward students, with assumptions that AI has led to students never completing their own assignments or having their own creative thoughts. As a university writing instructor, I have found these concerns to be largely unfounded. My students are finding their own authentic voices and producing original work, while using AI as a tool to help them meet learning outcomes in ways that comply with university research ethics. In the era of AI-when assignments, thoughts, and opinions can be easily outsourced to generative AI-it is critical that students understand the importance and value of having their own original thoughts and opinions, and the dangers of outsourcing them to an algorithm. Yet, encouraging students to find and use their own authentic voices through a well-developed curriculum, one that both fosters student self-efficacy and incorporates ethical use of AI, can be a joyful endeavour for an instructor, as it ultimately leads to joy for students. This article introduces collegiate-level curricular activities, some involving the use of AI, that help foster the development of authentic student voices in the composition classroom.

TI AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in
   the GenAI Era
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID ACHIEVEMENT EMOTIONS; FEEDBACK
AB This paper argues that assessment reform in the generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) era should move beyond defensive approaches focused primarily on preventing misconduct or detecting AI use. Synthesizing scholarship on assessment validity, relational and compassionate assessment, third space theory, and AI agents, this conceptual paper proposes joyful assessment as a rigorous and learner-centered framework for assessment design in the GenAI era. Joyful assessment is defined as assessment that is safe, emotionally responsive, empowering, and supportive of student agency. The paper examines how AI agents designed for specific educational purposes can supportjoyful assessment by creating low-stakes opportunities for practice, feedback, reflection, personalization, and multimodal demonstration of learning. It further argues that when implemented within relational and ethically governed environments AI agents can help mediate third space assessment environments that connect formal curriculum with students' interests, experiences, and learning needs. The paper demonstrates these ideas through a practical example and concludes by identifying ethical considerations and future research directions related to responsible design, learner experience, equity, validity, and relational assessment practice.

TI Constructing Collective Joy: Slogans, Social Identity, and Extremism
   Prevention in Religious Education
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB While joy is increasingly valorized as a pedagogical instrument for identity formation, its collective manifestation as a bulwark against ideological fragility remains undertheorized. Moving beyond individualistic affective states, this phenomenological inquiry examines the relational "blooming" of joy- conceptualized through Ross Gay's notion of shared struggle and Gholdy Muhammad's culturally responsive framework-among female students at Pondok Pesantren Salafiyah Syafi'iyah Situbondo. Through in-depth engagement with 40 participants, the study deconstructs organizational slogans not as mere rhetorical devices, but as affective anchors that cultivate radical inclusion and collective efficacy.The findings reveal that the Pesantren'sresilience against extremist narratives does not emerge from explicit counter-pedagogy, but from an ontological model of "Asambung,"a unique relational connectedness that integrates vertical (tauhidic), genealogical, and contextual dimensions of the self. Unlike Western positive psychology's emphasis on subjective experience, Asambung situates the individual within a profound network of transcendence and communal duty. This study argues that joy-centred pedagogy, mediated through these relational speech acts, effectively fills the identity voids targeted by extremist ideologies. This research offers cross-cultural expansions of counselling theory-including the Asambung model of triadic relational identity and the concept of Joyful Accountability-positioning collective joy as a protective mechanism against extremism.

TI Happiness as a Component of Recovering Motivation and Resiliency in
   Disaster-Prone Philippine Academic Settings
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
AB While educational disaster response typically prioritizes infrastructure restoration, there remains a critical deficit in psychosocial interventions that cultivate joy to address recurrent climate trauma. This study investigates the utility of happiness dispositions (joy, humour, satisfaction) as culturally mediated pedagogical resources for recovering academic motivation and resiliency among learners in disaster-prone regions. Using a qualitative exploratory design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 tertiary students selected via purposive sampling in high-risk zones, and analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that a joyful classroom climate is a vital foundational element. Establishing psychological safety acts as a catalyst, shifting students' neurobiology out of "survival mode" and freeing cognitive resources for learning. Emergent themes indicate culturally grounded humour and teacher relatability function as cognitive scaffolds for emotional anchoring. Aligning positive affect with academic material enhances retention while deconstructing fear-based academic hierarchies. This relational process, rooted in kapwa (shared identity), allows participants to temporarily suspend their survivor narratives and reclaim their student identities. joy-centred, trauma-informed teaching, emphasizing that relational authenticity and positive psychological capital are critical for sustainable academic continuity and localized teacher preparation.

AB The current educational context, characterized by increasingly diverse learner profiles, makes classroom behaviour management particularly complex. This study is based on a survey of 76 secondary school teachers from various disciplines who work with students exhibiting behavioural difficulties. TI Cultivating Joy Through Inclusion: Teachers' Practices for Supporting
   Young Learners with Dyslexia in Zimbabwean Mainstream Classrooms
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID FRAMEWORK; STUDENTS; DESIGN
AB Amid persistent resource shortages and exclusionary instructional practices, learners with dyslexia in mainstream classrooms are often portrayed through deficit-focused narratives that emphasise struggle and remediation. This study examines how joy functions as a pedagogical tool within inclusive teaching strategies in Zimbabwean primary schools. The study adopted a qualitative design involving twenty-four (24) primary school teachers from Chivi District, selected through convenience sampling based on their experience teaching learners with dyslexia across Grades 1 to 7. Data were generated through classroom observations and semi-structured interviews, enabling an in-depth exploration of teachers' practices and perspectives. These practices enhanced learner participation and agency while also strengthening teachers' professional commitment and sense of purpose within challenging contexts. The analysis reveals that joy is actively produced through deliberate inclusive teaching choices that challenge deficit-based models of disability. By foregrounding joy in inclusive education, the study contributes to discussions on justice-oriented pedagogy and reframes inclusion as a space of possibility rather than mere accommodation. Overall, the study argues that a joy-centred approach offers a valuable pathway for promoting both learner development and teacher resilience in mainstream classrooms.

TI Cultivating Joy Through Making: A Joy-Centred Pedagogical Study of
   Makerspaces in Primary Education
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB This study examines how joy is cultivated in a primary school Makerspace through the implementation of joy-centred pedagogy. While innovative learning environments are often assumed to naturally generate positive emotional experiences, limited research has investigated the pedagogical conditions that intentionally foster joyful learning in primary education contexts. Grounded in experiential learning theory, positive psychology, self-determination theory, and maker education, the study adopts a design-based research approach to explore how structured learning experiences can support the emergence of joy during hands-on learning activities. The intervention was conducted in a primary school Makerspace where students engaged in collaborative project-based tasks involving design, experimentation, and iterative problem-solving. Data were collected through student surveys, classroom observations, and reflective artifacts and analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. The findings reveal that joy was cultivated through four interrelated pedagogical conditions: meaningful challenge, collaborative interaction, learner autonomy, and opportunities for creative expression. These conditions enabled students to experience curiosity, confidence, and a sense of accomplishment while persisting in complex learning tasks. The study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that joy is not merely an emotional outcome of engaging activities but a pedagogically designable mechanism that supports meaningful participation and sustained engagement in learning environments.

TI Joy as Epistemic Energy: How Emotional-Epistemic Interactions Enhance
   Scientific Sense-Making, Conceptual Understanding, and Student Agency
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID BUILD THEORY; CLASSROOM; ENGAGEMENT; TEACHER; SCIENCE; SCHOOL
AB Amid increasing student disengagement, emotional distress, and performance-driven science instruction, this paper examines joy-centred pedagogy as a critical mechanism for fostering students' scientific sense-making and agency. Drawing on sociocultural and epistemic perspectives in science education, the study conceptualizes joy not as a peripheral emotional outcome but as an embodied, relational, and renewable epistemic resource that energizes learning. Using a mixed-methods design, data were collected from secondary science classrooms implementing inquiry-based, joy-centred instructional practices. Quantitative analyses examined the relationships among students' experienced joy, scientific agency, epistemic engagement, and conceptual understanding, while qualitative data illuminated how joy emerged through collaborative inquiry, productive struggle, and engagement with uncertainty. Structural equation modelling revealed that joy significantly predicted students' agency and epistemic engagement, which in turn mediated conceptual understanding. Qualitative findings further demonstrated that joy functioned as a form of collective care, enabling students to take intellectual risks, persist through difficulty, and experience science as meaningful rather than merely performative. The study argues that joy-centred pedagogy reframes scientific rigour as epistemic vigour, offering a powerful response to contemporary educational ill-being. Implications are discussed for science curriculum design, equity-oriented instruction, and the cultivation of learning environments where students can flourish through curiosity, solidarity, and shared sense-making.

TI From Abstract to Alive: Joy-Centred Professional Development for
   Teaching Genetics in Secondary Schools
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID PLACE-BASED EDUCATION; SCIENCE
AB Traditional approaches to teaching genetics in life sciences have often failed to equip teachers with effective strategies for engaging learners with complex and abstract concepts. In contexts marked by teacher burnout, learner disengagement, and persistent conceptual difficulty, there is a growing need for professional development approaches that empower teachers with effective teaching and learning strategies. This article explores joy-centred pedagogy as a suitable approach to professional development of life sciences teachers through a university-school partnership. Guided by Placed-Based Education Theory, the study examines how outdoor, community-based teaching strategies supported teachers' understanding of genetics and revitalized their pedagogical practice. The professional development initiative involved demonstrations and hands-on learning in a local garden and cattle kraal, where teachers engaged in simulations of genetic crosses using natural materials and observed inherited characteristics in cattle. A qualitative design employed purposive sampling of 20 Grade 10-12 life sciences teachers. The thematic analysis of data revealed renewed confidence, heightened motivation, and deeper conceptual understanding, as complex terminology became accessible through experiential engagement. The findings suggest that experiential, joy-centred professional development fosters understanding of complex terminology. Outdoor and community-based learning emerges as a culturally responsive and transformative strategy for teaching challenging life sciences topics.

TI Unpacking EFL students' engagement with GAI in digital multimodal
   composing
SO LANGUAGE LEARNING & TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE digital multimodal composing; generative artificial intelligence;
   engagement; EFL curriculum
AB While existing studies underscore the potential of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) to streamline digital multimodal composing (DMC) and elevate product quality, research systematically synthesizing learners' multi-dimensional engagement with GAI in DMC remains limited. Adopting a qualitative research method, this study investigated eight Chinese EFL undergraduates' cognitive, behavioral, and emotional engagement with GAI in DMC and the influencing factors. Data sources included semi-structured interviews, written reflections, screenshots, and final DMC products. The findings showed that, behaviorally, students leveraged different GAI tools to accomplish seven major goals, including textual content generation, analytical processing, content reorganization, content refinement, translation, task management, and multimodal content generation. Cognitively, students implemented four strategies to optimize GAI's unsatisfactory output, namely, manual refining, revising prompts, negotiating with GAI, and leveraging the strengths and offsetting weaknesses of different GAI tools. Students expressed both positive and negative emotions towards GAI integration in DMC due to its affordances and limitations. Both individual and contextual factors influenced students' engagement, including learner agency, GAI literacy, L2 proficiency, peer recognition, division of labor, and contextual limitations. Based on the findings, we propose a Model ofLearner Engagement in GAI-assisted DMC and provide actionable insights for optimizing GAI-integrated DMC pedagogy.

TI Transcultural care in researcher training: internationalization through
   the lens of the Sunrise model O cuidado transcultural na formação do
   pesquisador: a internacionalização pela lente do modelo Sunrise
SO REVISTA IBERO-AMERICANA DE ESTUDOS EM EDUCACAO
LA English
DT Article
DE Portugal; international educational exchange; health postgraduate
   programs; education; cross-cultural care
AB Internationalization is a strategic process for the transformation of higher education, as it allows for the expansion of science beyond its own geographical boundaries. However, because it constitutes a transcultural experience, it requires researchers to adapt. The study aimed to analyze the experience of internationalization and its contribution to the scientific, professional, and personal development process, from the perspective of Leininger's model of transcultural care. It examines the experience of a Brazilian PhD student at a Portuguese institution of higher education, funded by the Coordination for the Improvement of Higher Education Personnel (CAPES), from October 2025 to March 2026. The results are presented by applying the Sunrise model across four levels: worldview; the individual and influencing factors; knowledge and systems; and decisions and actions. Internationalization was a complex transitional experience, emerging as a process of identity formation.

TI Linguistic corpora as a pedagogical tool in translator training: an
   exploratory study in the Mexican context
SO REVISTA IBERO-AMERICANA DE ESTUDOS EM EDUCACAO
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; innovation in education; linguistic corpora;
   translation competence; translator education
ID DESIGN
AB The integration of linguistic corpora into university translator education represents a promising strategy for strengthening translation competence. This study examined their impact on the development of instrumental and strategic sub-competences through a mixed-methods quasi-experimental design with pre-test and post-test measures, complemented by translation logs and perception questionnaires. Participants from three Mexican higher education institutions completed translation tasks before and after an instructional intervention based on corpus use. The results revealed statistically significant improvements, accompanied by large effect sizes across all comparisons. Qualitative analyses also identified changes in documentation strategies, problem-solving processes, and metacognitive reflection throughout the translation task. Overall, the findings support the pedagogical value of linguistic corpora as instructional resources for fostering translation competence in higher education.

TI Between languages and borders: intercultural education on the
   Brazil-Bolivia border and the limits of the Brazilian National Education
   Guidelines (LDB) in Mato Grosso
SO REVISTA IBERO-AMERICANA DE ESTUDOS EM EDUCACAO
LA English
DT Article
DE intercultural bilingual education; border education; chiquitano
   indigenou people; educational policies; decoloniality
AB The study investigated how public policies aimed at intercultural bilingual education have been implemented in basic education within international border contexts, focusing on the state of Mato Grosso. The research is grounded in the understanding that border territories are marked by intense cultural, social, and linguisticflows, shaping complex and plural educational realities. The diversity present in these spaces reveals both possibilities for intercultural pedagogical practices and challenges related to teacher education, curriculum organization, and the implementation of educational policies that are responsive to local specificities. Methodologically, the research adopted a qualitative documentary approach, articulated with critical discourse analysis and a decolonial epistemological perspective. Official documents, Brazilian educational legislation, and curriculum guidelines that guide education for cultural and linguistic diversity were analyzed. The results indicate that, although there have been normative advances, limitations persist in the application of the Brazilian National Education Guidelines and Framework Law (LDB) and other national policies in addressing the intercultural demands of border schools, revealing tensions between legal prescriptions and concrete pedagogical practices.

TI Toward Other Grammars: Anagrammatical Designs Beyond the American School
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE learning environments; organization theory/change; race; educational
   reform; human development; cultural analysis; Black; Native; America;
   life; grammar; learning; school
ID EDUCATION; ORGANIZATION
AB How might education scholars (re)design places of learning to contribute to the wellbeing of young people and the natural world on which we depend? Drawing on Black, Native, and critical studies in education, we offer two conceptual interventions to studies on school reform and organizational (re)design. First, we connect Spillers's notion of the "American grammar" to the "grammar of schooling" through a construct we call the "American grammar of schooling." This combined concept distills how antiblack and colonial hierarchies of human being underpin what we commonly take for granted as school. Second, we connect Sharpe's notion of "anagrammatical Blackness" to introduce "anagrammatical designs," or learning spaces that unsettle the American grammar of schooling and (re)generate relations that sustain life, land, and kinship. We challenge how such designs are often dismissed as "gibberish" or "nonsense" and highlight examples of anagrammatical designs already-in-motion. We conclude by exploring other grammars that offer transformative possibilities for education.

TI Rethinking Gestalts and the Natural Language Acquisition Framework:
   Advancing Construction Grammar Approaches for Autistic AAC-Aided
   Language Learners
SO AUTISM & DEVELOPMENTAL LANGUAGE IMPAIRMENTS
LA English
DT Article
DE Gestalt language; GLP; natural language acquisition; NLA; AAC; autism
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; INTERACTIONAL RESOURCE; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES;
   TYPICAL DEVELOPMENT; SENTENCE DIVERSITY; FORMULAIC LANGUAGE; JOINT
   ATTENTION; CHILDREN; USAGE; COMPREHENSION
AB Background & Aims The Natural Language Acquisition (NLA) framework and discourse on "gestalt language processing" (GLP) have gained substantial visibility in clinical communities and are increasingly shaping intervention for autistic children, including recommendations for augmentative and alternative communication (AAC). Despite this uptake, NLA's definitions, theoretical assumptions, and developmental claims remain contested in the spoken domain and have not been empirically examined in AAC.Main Contribution In this article, we examine three assumptions central to NLA: (1) that words are the fundamental building blocks of language, (2) that autistic learners are "gestalt" processors, and (3) that neurotypical "analytic" processors acquire language one word at a time. We contrast these assumptions with a Construction Grammar (CXG) account of language acquisition, challenge the NLA-informed AAC recommendation to program "gestalts" onto a single AAC button, and outline the potential unintended consequences that make this practice highly concerning. Finally, we evaluate the implications of exporting other NLA treatment recommendations to AAC (e.g., restrictions on verbs, grammar, recasts) and outline how a CXG-informed approach better guides the development of AAC supports.Conclusions and Implications Transferring NLA protocols to AAC introduces avoidable clinical risks. By contrast, a CxG-informed approach aligns with prevailing language acquisition theory and established AAC best practices by emphasizing robust systems, morphosyntactically complete modeling, recasts, sentence diversity, and structured interaction that makes constructions salient and extendable. We conclude that the relevant clinical task is not to classify learners as gestalt or analytic processors but to design interactional environments that accommodate learner and device constraints to make salient and accessible the patterns replete in language to support language development.

TI Multi-Modal Virtual Reality in Engineering Education: A Design Case
   Study of Fostering Situational Interest through Project-Based Learning
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE multi-modal learning; situational interest; project-based learning
   (PjBL); student engagement; cave automatic virtual environments (CAVE)
ID INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; ENVIRONMENTS; ENGAGEMENT; STUDENTS; MODEL
AB Engineering students struggle with abstract concepts and theory-practice integration, yet few studies systematically examine how to design virtual reality (VR) learning environments that sustain engagement beyond initial novelty effects. Multi-modal approaches that strategically integrate different technological affordances offer promising but underexplored solutions. This design case study demonstrates the development and implementation of a multi-modal VR learning environment integrating immersive Cave Automatic Virtual Environments (CAVE), non-immersive MATLAB simulations, and artificial intelligence (AI) motion tracking within project-based learning (PjBL). We investigate how different technological modalities can be strategically orchestrated to support situational interest development in undergraduate engineering education. We designed and implemented a four-week "Biomechanics of a Pitch" project in a Strength of Materials course, engaging 20 undergraduate mechanical engineering students. Using an exploratory case study approach with convergent mixed-methods data collection, we measured presence, representation fidelity, and situational interest through validated instruments (alpha = 0.92-0.93) and focus groups. Data was analyzed through reliabil-ity analyses, descriptive statistics, and thematic analysis to understand design effectiveness and student experiences. The multi-modal design enabled distinct complementary techno-logical affordances: CAVE excelled in spatial presence (alpha = 0.93) and immersive understand-ing (M = 4.2, SD = 0.8), MATLAB supported analytical thinking and pedagogical usefulness, while AI motion tracking created personalized connections. Student interest evolved from pre-experience curiosity through maintained engagement during multi-modal experiences to post-experience learning motivation. Qualitative data revealed how strategic modality transi-tions sustained engagement beyond novelty effects. We present an integrated framework syn-thesizing interest development theory with multi-modal VR design principles, demonstrating how theoretically grounded VR implementations move beyond novelty effects through stra-tegic technological orchestration. The study contributes a design framework, evidence-based design checklist, and practical implementation guidelines for engineering educators seeking to create effective VR-enhanced learning experiences.

TI Strategic Importance of Education in Cybersecurity
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE cyber security; cybersecurity education; engineering pedagogy; SWOT;
   security awareness
AB This paper examines the strategic importance of cybersecurity education as a pedagogical and managerial mechanism for strengthening organisational resilience. Responding to the need for practice-orientated engineering pedagogy, the paper formulates a guiding research question: How can role-specific cybersecurity education be selected, justified, and evaluated so that it supports resilient behaviour across organisational levels? The study combines a structured narrative review of cybersecurity education and awareness approaches with a transparent SWOT-based analytical framework. SWOT is used as a managerial self-assessment tool for identifying strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in both the general cybersecurity environment and the human-factor dimension. The paper distinguishes gamification from games, explains the rationale for selecting educational approaches, and proposes operational criteria for translating SWOT findings into training requirements. The contribution is intended for educators, cybersecurity managers, and organisational leaders who design or evaluate cybersecurity awareness programmes in engineering-orientated, technical, and socio-technical environments.

TI AI-Based Learning Analytics and Real-Time Monitoring for IoT-Enabled
   Smart Laboratory of Engineering Education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Internet of Things (IoT); smart laboratory; engineering education;
   real-time monitoring; learning analytics; edge AI
AB Engineering laboratories play a significant role in facilitating problem-based learning across electrical, environmental, computer, and interdisciplinary engineering programs; however, most lab sessions still rely on physical attendance, delayed grading, limited equipment references, and little visibility into student engagement. This lack of visibility compromises instructors' ability to identify learning barriers, unsafe conditions, uneven resource use, and at-risk students during lab sessions. An Internet of Things (IoT) smart lab framework is proposed that uses real-time sensor data, edge processing, and cloud storage to support learning analytics for improved operational and pedagogical decisions. The framework integrates data from environmental sensors, smart equipment, workstation logs, access control, and learning platforms to create a continuous data stream. An analytic layer processes this data using structured event learning and sequence modeling to estimate engagement, detect at-risk sessions, identify equipment bottlenecks, and enable timely intervention. A prototype simulated undergraduate engineering lab is developed to evaluate latency, reliability, predictive performance, and interpretability. Results show 93.4% engagement accuracy, 0.914 macro-F1, 0.887 AUROC for early risk detection, and 1.8 seconds median latency, outperforming temporal and non-temporal baselines. These findings demonstrate that multimodal sensing with explainable AI improves operational visibility and educational analytics. The framework defines the engineering lab as a cyber-physical learning environment rather than a collection of devices, supporting safer, more efficient, and data-driven learning across engineering disciplines.

TI Exploring the Ethical Boundaries of AI Use in Secondary Vocational
   Education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence (AI); vocational education; ethics in education;
   academic dishonesty; digital competencies; secondary technical schools
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; STUDENTS ATTITUDES; PERCEPTIONS; CHATGPT;
   SKILLS
AB The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education presents both significant opportunities and complex ethical challenges. This study examines the use of AI among learners attending secondary technical and vocational schools, with a particular focus on the boundary between legitimate learning support and academic dishonesty. A quantitative questionnaire survey was conducted with 1,745 learners from Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland. The collected data were analysed using descriptive statistics and a thematic analysis of open-ended responses. The results indicate widespread use of AI tools among the surveyed learners. Most respondents reported regular use of AI to understand learning materials, generate texts, complete assignments and support project work. Many respondents reported confidence in evaluating AI-generated content, suggesting a perceived level of digital literacy and critical awareness. Nevertheless, open-ended responses revealed several forms of academically dishonest AI use, particularly for generating code, writing essays, preparing presentations and completing tasks without meaningful cognitive engagement. Thematic analysis identified key motivations such as time efficiency and pragmatic task management, alongside a nuanced awareness of the ethical boundary between legitimate assistance and misconduct. The findings highlight the urgent need for pedagogical approaches that promote responsible and ethical use of AI. Moreover, the study reinforces the view that, in an increasingly technology-driven educational landscape, competencies in interacting with AI, such as formulating effective prompts, verifying outputs, and engaging in critical evaluation, are becoming essential skills for vocational school graduates.

TI Undergraduate Research Training and Generic Competencies in Engineering
   Graduates
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate research training; generic competencies; research-based
   learning (RLB); engineering education; science; technology; engineering;
   and mathematics (STEM)
ID RESEARCH CULTURE; SKILLS; EDUCATION; IMPACT
AB Higher education programs are embracing curricular models that incorporate active teaching-learning methodologies to foster students' active participation in knowledge building, based on competency-based training. Research-based learning (RBL) stands out as an active methodology that can be used at various academic levels, including undergraduate. In this context, the present research explores the contribution of undergraduate research training to the process of developing generic competencies in engineering students. The study focuses on the perceptions of a group of employers and graduates from a Peruvian higher education institution. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, as interviews and surveys were applied. The study had a descriptive purpose with a concurrent design. The findings suggest that undergraduate research training is perceived as supporting the development of generic competencies such as research, teamwork, effective communication, analytical and critical thinking, adaptability, digital literacy, intellectual curiosity, and lifelong learning (LL). Overall, the results highlight undergraduate research training, implemented through RBL, as an effective strategy associated with the development and strengthening of generic competencies and the alignment of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) education with labor market demands, while underscoring the importance of consolidating an institutional research culture within competency-based curricula.

TI Improving Problem-Solving Skills and Learning Retention in a Thai
   Electrical Circuit Laboratory Using Flipped Classroom, Augmented
   Reality, and Microlearning
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality; electrical circuit laboratory; flipped classroom;
   learning achievement; microlearning; problem-solving skills
ID EDUCATION
AB This study aimed to develop and evaluate a flipped, microlearning, and augmented reality model to enhance undergraduate engineering students' conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills in an electrical circuit laboratory course. The participants consisted of 43 first-year engi- neering students, divided into an experimental group (n = 21) and a control group (n = 22). The experimental group was instructed using the integrated model, while the control group received traditional instruction. Research instruments included a learning achievement test, a problem-solving skills rubric, and a satisfaction questionnaire, all of which demonstrated acceptable validity and reliability. Data were analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and mixed ANOVA. The findings indicated that students in the experimental group significantly outperformed those in the control group in both learning achievement (p < .05) and problem-solving skills (p < .01). In addition, the experimental group demonstrated greater learn- ing retention at two weeks after instruction. These results suggest that integrating augmented reality and microlearning within a flipped classroom framework effectively supports conceptual understanding and enhances problem-solving skills in engineering education. The integrated model provides a practical instructional approach for improving laboratory-based learning in science and engineering contexts. This study extends existing research by providing an instruc- tional framework that supports both cognitive and experiential learning in higher education.

TI in AI-Supported Collaborative Programming: Mediating Roles of Growth
   Mindset and Mastery Experience
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE achievement goal; growth mindset; mastery experience; self-efficacy;
   programming
ID SELF-EFFICACY; ACHIEVEMENT
AB This study designed an AI-integrated collaborative problem-based learning (CPBL) course aimed to bolster programming self-efficacy among undergraduate and to elucidate the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive self-efficacy. A total of 179 Taiwanese undergraduates participated in an 18-week intervention that integrated AI toolkits, CPBL frameworks, and instructional scaffolding to facilitate interdisciplinary application. To achieve our goals, two instruments were developed to measure programming-specific achieve-ment goals and mindsets. The results indicated that the AI-supported CPBL environment effectively fostered a growth mindset, mastery experiences, and self-efficacy in programming. Mediation model analysis revealed that growth mindset and mastery experience functioned as dual mediators linking achievement goal orientation to self-efficacy. Notably, mastery goals exerted a markedly stronger influence on self-efficacy compared to performance goals. The findings highlight the necessity of prioritizing mastery-oriented pedagogy in the design of AI curricula.

TI Re-Engineering Supply Chain Education: A Theoretical Framework for
   Integrating Financial Asymmetry and Systems Thinking
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING PEDAGOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; systems thinking; problem-based learning;
   financial bullwhip effect; supply chain finance
ID MACHINE LEARNING-MODELS; PREDICTION
AB Modern industrial and systems engineering curricula excel at teaching students to mitigate physical supply-side disruptions, yet frequently fail to address the intra-supply-chain allocation of financial distress. This theoretical paper proposes a novel, problem-based learning curriculum framework designed to bridge the gap between operational logistics and finan-cial risk-shifting. It critiques the pedagogical reliance on traditional bankruptcy prediction models, demonstrating how they systematically misclassify capital-intensive original equip-ment manufacturers (OEMs) into distress zones due to the structural liabilities of captive financial divisions. Grounded in systems thinking and Kolb's experiential learning theory, the proposed framework introduces dynamic industry benchmarks into the classroom, spe-cifically utilizing the Strouhal Credibility Index (SCI). By structuring a pedagogical module around the 2020-2022 automotive crisis, and utilizing descriptive statistical comparisons rather than complex econometrics, this framework equips engineering educators with an accessible blueprint to teach the financial bullwhip effect. This ensures future engineering managers understand the structural vulnerabilities embedded within hierarchical supply chains and the limits of OEM-driven supply chain finance.

TI SUPPORTING CONCEPTUAL AND COGNITIVE PROGRESSION: INTEGRATING FLIPPED
   DESIGN AND PEER INSTRUCTION INTO AN UPPER-SECONDARY PHYSICS TUTORIAL
   MODEL
SO JOURNAL OF BALTIC SCIENCE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE flipped design; upper-secondary physics; peer instruction; SOLO
   taxonomy; physics tutorials
AB A tutorial model for upper-secondary physics that combines peer instruction and a flipped design was developed to replace a lecture-based teaching approach. Implemented in two upper-secondary schools (N = 149), the intervention integrated pre-class preparation, structured worksheets, demonstrations, peer discussions, and mini-laboratories. Learning outcomes were evaluated through pre/post-tests, SOLO taxonomy coding, and semi-structured interviews, with test and interview protocols thoroughly examined for content validity (IOC = 0.73) and reliability (KR-20 = 0.78). A paired-samples t-test indicated significant improvements in students' conceptual understanding and problem-solving skills (p < .001, Cohen's d = 3.72 and 5.21), alongside substantial normalized gains (g = 0.76 and 0.77). Consistent with these quantitative results, SOLO analysis revealed a progression from prestructural and unistructural reasoning toward predominantly relational reasoning across the three physics topics. Thematic analysis of interview data (n = 34) further suggested that scaffolded worksheets and collaborative sense-making appeared to help students overcome cognitive bottlenecks, while also showing positive links to their engagement and confidence. Together, these findings suggest that a tutorial model integrating peer instruction and a flipped design can offer a viable pedagogical strategy for supporting conceptual and cognitive progression in physics.

TI Beyond Online Course Evaluations: Student-Led Focus Groups for
   Curricular Feedback
SO PERSPECTIVES ON MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID EDUCATIONAL ALLIANCE
AB Purpose: Medical student curricular evaluation is both beneficial and required. Most medical schools rely on online questionnaires for evaluations, but these are often overlooked or completed haphazardly. We describe the implementation of focus groups as a supplemental form of curricular assessment and evaluate students' and faculty members' attitudes towards this novel approach. Method: Ten randomly selected students were assigned to eight focus groups regarding three different preclerkship courses. Following the completion of focus groups, interviews were conducted with students who participated in them, course directors who received the focus group reports, and administrators who oversaw the preclerkship curriculum and the implementation of the focus group program. The semi-structured interviews were then analyzed using inductive thematic analysis, with initial codes generated from the data and subsequent interpretation informed by prior literature on feedback relationships and curricular program evaluation. Results: Interviews were conducted with 17 students, 5 faculty members, and 3 administrators. Participants highlighted key themes related to trust, engagement, collaboration, and the learning environment. Students described the focus groups as a safe space and said they enjoyed thinking critically about improvements. Faculty perceived the thematic content of focus group reports to be comparable to course evaluation summaries from established online forms despite concerns for a smaller sample size. Conclusions: Focus groups are a novel supplemental tool that can complement existing evaluation mechanisms. Engaging students through focus groups can improve feedback and advance medical school curricula, resulting in a more responsive and adaptive approach to education.
